speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Mr. GEORGE PARENT (Quebec West) presented the first report of the SelectStanding Committee on Standing Orders as follows:
In accordance with the order of reference of Your Honourable House of the 27th of March, 1924, your Committee have had under consideration a petition signed,-
On behalf of the Presbyterian Church in Canada, by Alfred Gandier, Moderator of the General Assembly of the Presbyterian Church in Canada;
On behalf of the Methodist Church by S. D. Chown, General Superintendent, The Methodist Church;
On behalf of the Congregational Union of Canada, by J. Lambert Alexander, Chairman, The Congregational Union of Canada;
praying for the passing of an act to incorporate them under the name of The United Church of Canada; also the fourth report of the Examiner of Petitions in reference thereto.
Your committee, after hearing counsel for both sides, were able to satisfactorily determine that the notices were published in twenty-seven newspapers in the various provinces of Canada, as well as in the church papers of the three denominations affected; and as evidence was submitted to the effect that copies of the proposed bill have been distributed to every Presbyterian minister and elder.in Canada, your committee are of the opinion that the requirements of the rules of the House have been complied with, and find that the notices as published have been sufficient.
Your committee have also considered the petitions contesting the authority of the Moderator of the Presbyterian Church to bind the said Presbyterian Church in Canada, and have come to the conclusion that the questions involved in said petitions should be taken up and considered by any committee to which the bill may be referred in due course.
All which is respectfully submitted.
Chairman.
Mr. PARENT moved that the report be concurred in.
Motion agreed to.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the Orders of the day.

maintopic: MIGRANTS FROM CANADA TO UNITED STATES
speechtext:
I desire to bring to the attention of the government a news item which appeared in the Manitoba Free Press some days ago which reads:
The Budget-Mr. Robb

Washington, March 27.-The new Immigration bill was reported to the Senate this afternoon, and will be given the right-of-way next week. The chief item of interest to Canada is the restriction upon immigrants from Canada not born in the Dominion. No quota barrier is erected against native-born Canadians, but other immigrants from Canada will be treated as though coming from the land of their birth. Thus, a Canadian citizen born in England would be refused admission if the British quota were exhausted.
Senator Colt, Republican, Rhode Island, chairman of the senate immigration committee, interviewed by the Free Press this evening, said: "The underlying principle in the bill is restriction of immigration from all countries except our sister nations on this continent. We find, however, that European immigrants evade the quota provision of the Immigration Act by colonizing in contiguous countries, notably Cuba, and then come into the United States as citizens of such country. To stop this we provided all immigrants shall be treated as coming from their native land. We had no complaint about Canada, but the provision is general, and, of course, applies to Canadian citizens not born on this continent."
I desire to ask the government if they have any information which they can give to the House as to whether this discrimination against naturalized citizens is to be carried on.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Immigration and Colonization):
speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization
maintopic: MIGRANTS FROM CANADA TO UNITED STATES
speechtext: Until my hon. friend (Mr. Euler) brought this matter to our attention, I had not had any notice of it. I shall look into the matter to which it refers, and make a reply in a day or two.

I do not wish to be
critical, but, according to Rule 17C, on Thursdays and Fridays when the Order of the Day is called for the House to go into committee of supply or of ways and means, Mr. Speaker shall leave the chair without putting any question. I suppose if I were to take the letter of the law, I would have to leave the chair, and the budget speech would be delivered in the committee of the whole House. I think I am living up to the traditions of the House by putting the question and proceeding as we have always proceeded before this rule came into force.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in presenting the annual financial statement to parliament, I cannot refrain from expressing what I know to be the unanimous feeling of this House, our profound regret that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) is unable to be present to-day to deliver it himself. Last year that right hon. gentleman delivered his seventeenth budget speech, a record, I believe, unequalled by any other Minister of Finance within the Empire. When, upon the assumption of office by the present administration, the right hon. gentleman returned to his former post as Minister of Finance, it was at a critical period in the history of Canada. I am sure that the House will agree with me when I say that since then the Right Hon. W. S. Fielding has discharged his important and onerous duties with that ability, integrity and courage always characteristic of him during his long and distinguished career. Hon. gentlemen of all

The Budget-Mr. Robb
parties in this House will, I know, join with me in wishing him a speedy recovery from his present illness and an early return to his public duties.
Fiscal Year 1922-23-Revenue
The Public Accounts for 1922-23 were submitted to parliament during this present session. The consolidated revenues or ordinary receipts obtained during that year were $394,614,900, an increase of $12,662,513.01 over the previous year.
Other receipts, amounting to $8,479,310.30, which included $8,199,333.31 received from the Imperial government to cover exchange on repayments in London to the Dominion of Canada from July, 1920, to August 2, 1921, brought the gross revenue to $403,094,210.30.
Expenditure 1922-23
The expenditure side shows $332,293,732.09 for ordinary expenses. Capital, demobliza-tion and other charges amounted to $18,314,814.63, thus making the total disbursements for that year $350,608,546.72.
The surplus of revenue over total disbursements left $52,485,663.58 available for railways, Canadian Government Merchant Marine and other obligations amounting to $84,126,730.59. Of this amount $77,862,348.23 was required for railways and $5,979,856.08 for the Canadian Government Merchant Marine. The outcome of the year resulted in an increase of $31,641,067.01 to the public debt.
Fiscal Year 1923-24
Coming now to the year 1923-24 which has just closed, I might say that some time will elapse before all the returns for that year will come to hand and allow of definite results being determined. We can, however, make a fairly close estimate which should not differ materially from the actual figures when the books are closed.
Estimated Revenue 1923-24
By adding to the actual revenue received by the Department of Finance, up to and including 31st March last, the estimated amount of revenue yet to come, the accounts for that year, when finally closed, will show a total revenue of about $396,000,000, being an increase of $1,500,000 over the revenue of 1922-23.
The estimated revenue from customs duties will be $121,800,000, aj^ increase of $3,700,000 over the previous year. From excise duties we expect $38,200,000, an increase of about $2,500,000. The estimated revenue from excise taxes will be $121,000,000, an increase of about $14,500,000. From income taxes we estimate $53,750,000, a decrease of about $6,000,000 as compared with the previous year. From delayed business profits taxes we will receive some $4,650,000, a decrease of $8,381,000. We estimate a revenue from interest on investments of $11,700,000, being a decrease of about $4,700,000, which is accounted for by the reduction in 1922 of some $56,000,000 in the indebtedness of the Imperial government to Canada.
Estimated Expenditure 1923-24
Turning now to expenditures, it is estimated that when all accounts are closed, the expenditure for the year on ordinary account will be $328,250,000, a decrease as compared with the previous year of $4,000,000.
Estimated Surplus of Ordinary Revenue over
Ordinary Expenditure, 1923-24
Taking the estimated revenue for the year ended March 31, 1924, as $396,000,000, and the estimated expenditure chargeable to Consolidated Fund as $328,250,000, there will be a surplus of revenue over the ordinary expenditure of $67,750,000, available for capital, special and other obligations.
Capital Expenditures, 1923-24
Capital expenditure for public works, including Marine department, will amount tc $3,865,000, and capital expenditure for Railways and Canals, $8,305,000, making a total capital expenditure of $12,170,000, an increase of $2,362,000 over the previous year.
Special Expenditures, 1923-24
Special expenditures will amount to $8,390,000, of which $740,000 will be required for
demobilization accounts, and $7,650,000 for discount and cost of loan flotations.
Railway Loans
Parliament at its last session authorised $74,550,000 for loans to the Canadian National Railway Company, to be made by way of cash, or by way of guarantee, or partly one way and partly the other. These alternative provisions for meeting railway obligations as

The Budget-Mr. Robb

voted by parliament were first authorised during the session of 1921.
In July, 1921, $25,000,1)00 was raised by way of guarantee for Canadian Northern railway purposes; and in September, 1921, a further amount of $25,000,000 was raised by way of guarantee for purposes of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, making in all $50,000,000 by way of guarantee chargeable against the loan vote for 1921-22. During the fiscal year 1922-23, the government was in a position to meet the railway requirements by way of loans in cash. During the fiscal year just ended, $24,550,000 was paid to the railways by way of cash. We received $768,336 as a refund against the amount advanced in 192122 for purchase of rails.
The vote for the fiscal year was charged with $24,550,000, and the balance of $50,000,000 was raised in February last by way of guarantee and held by the Minister of Finance in a trust account, payments being made from time to time as necessity arose.
I may say that when loans are made by way of cash, under the arrangements made by the former Minister of Finance, they are treated as non-active assets and are, therefore, not taken into account when determining the net public debt. Moneys raised by way of guarantee, which places the government in the position of an endorser, do not presently affect the public debt in any way, as they are indirect obligations.
The action taken by the former Minister of Finance in treating cash loans to the Canadian National Railways as non-active assets is, I think, a very proper procedure, especially when such loans are for the purpose of meeting deficits whenever incurred, and interest charges.
Where moneys are required for construction purposes to better equip the railways for increased earning powers, there is no question that such obligations might be considered as proper capital charges, and, if necessary, be met by way of guaranteeing the issue of railway securities.
The railway issue of February last, guaranteed by the Minister of Finance, was to meet capital charges. A substantial balance is still held in trust by the minister and will be available for the railways for such purposes during the year 1924-25.

The $22,500,000 issue of 1923 is the first equipment issue carrying the government's guarantee. The bonds are secured on the equipment purchased and, in addition, guaranteed under the Guarantee Act of 1923. This was done so as to make the security more attractive to investors and secure the highest price. Previous equipment issues were obligations of the company, specifically secured by the equipment, but without any government guarantee.
Public Debt
Turning now to the public debt. On March 31, 1923, our net public debt stood at $2,453,776,868.74. Our estimated ordinary revenue for the year just closed is $396,000,000. Our estimated ordinary expenditures of $328,-
250,000,	and capital expenditures $12,170,000; special expenditures $8,390,000; railway loans $23,781,664; Canadian Government Merchant Marine loans $1,500,000, and loans to Quebec Harbour Commission, which are treated as a non-active asset, $500,000, together with an amount of $621,987 carried on the books of the department for Victoria Shipowners, Limited, which it is proposed to treat as a non-active asset in the place of an active asset as heretofore make the total charges $375,213,651. Our surplus of ordinary revenue over these expenditures will therefore be $20,786,349 to be applied towards the reduction of the national debt as it stood on March 31, 1923. To this must be added $1,317,000, being the amount of sundry outstanding indebtedness cancelled during the past year, and a further amount of $8,305,760.37 received in settlement of an adjustment of acknowledged book debts between the Imperial and the Dominion governments. These two amounts, totalling $9,622,760.37, together with the $20,788,349 surplus of revenue over total expenditures, reduce our net public debt as of March 31, 1923, by the amount of $30,409,109.37.
On March 28 last an adjustment of acknowledged book debts between the Imperial and the Dominion governments was effected. The Imperial government as shown by the books of the Department of Finance, were indebted to us in the amount of $66,779,597.42. On the other hand, the Imperial gov-

ernment held our bonds to an amount of $67,207,351.17, of which $2,000,000 were 3i per cent bonds maturing 1925-28, and $65,207,351.17 were 4i per cent bonds maturing 1925-45, the bonds being part of an issue made by Canada to the Imperial government in 1916. Negotiations were undertaken and settlement made by offsetting bonds issued to the Imperial government against their indebtedness to Canada. The unmatured bond issues were taken at the rate of 92.91 for the 3i per cent issue and 87.48 for the 4jt per cent issue. A settlement was effected on a 5i per cent basis, being the rate of interest Canada is paying on her outstanding Victory loans from which the moneys were obtained for advances to the Imperial government. The value of the bonds at these rates was $58,901,590.80, being $8,305,760.37 under their face value.
Refunding Loan
On November 1, 1923, the 5i per cent five-year bonds of the 1918 Victory loan issue amounting to $172,459,650 matured. In September last tenders were asked for an issue of a five per cent refunding loan. The highest bid, from a Canadian syndicate, was accepted, namely, $53,000,000 five-year bonds at 96.75 and accrued interest and $147,000,000 twenty-year bonds at 96 and accrued interest. Arrangements were made with the syndicate to give to holders of the maturing bonds the privilege of converting their holdings into bonds of the refunding issue. The price to the public was 99 for the five-year bonds and 98.25 for the twenty-year bonds. The maturity date of the refunding loan is October 15, 1928, for the five-year bonds, and October 15, 1943, for the twenty-year bonds. It was stipulated that the syndicate should associate with themselves the recognized bond dealers in Canada. All commissions to banks and brokers, advertising expenses and all other charges usually included in flotation expenses, were borne by the syndicate. Holders of the matured bonds took advantage of the offer to the extent of $59,388,200, leaving a balance of $113,071,450 to be redeemed in cash.
Fiscal Year 1924-25
I come now to the fiscal year 1924-25. Estimates of revenue for the year upon which we have just entered cannot be made with any degree of accuracy. The revenue we would receive on the present basis of taxation would be materially affected by reductions in taxes which, in view of the most satisfactory outcome of the year just closed, it is proposed to submit to parliament. It is hoped, however, to offset any considerable reduction in the revenue by a most rigid economy in ex-78*
penditures. The estimates now before the House show a very substantial reduction as compared with the estimates of last year. We shall no doubt have supplementaries, but rigid economy will be exercised in their preparation; and in this the government hopes for and expects co-operation from all sections of Canada.

This brief statement showing the steady growth of Canadian trade with the nations of the world must be gratifying to Canadians.
During the fiscal year ended March 31, 1914-four months before the outbreak of the Great War-Canada had a total foreign trade of $1,074,631,222, with an excess of imports over exports of $163,756,774. To that extent the balance of trade was against Canada. The fiscal year ended March, 1922, shows a total foreign trade of $1,501,731,341. The difference between exports and imports~was only $6,122,677, but the balance was favourable to Canada. In the fiscal year ended March, 1923, we had a total foreign trade of $1,747,875,081, with a favourable balance of $142,716,593 over imports. In other words, Canadian foreign trade had increased 60 per cent over that of 1914, an unfavourable trade balance of $163,756,774 had been converted into a favourable balance of $142,716,593.
Returns for the eleven months ended February, 1924, indicate continued healthy growth of Canadian foreign trade. Already both imports and exports exceed those of 1923, and the balance of trade favourable to Canada on eleven months' business is $158,524,707. Statistics indicate that each succeeding year Canadians are increasing the percentage of products marketed in the finished or semifinished condition, thus providing more labour for our own people and higher class freight for Canadian railways.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF HON. J. A. ROBB, ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I rise, Mr. Speaker to move the adjournment of the debate, but before doing so I desire to make one or two observations. In the first place I want to congratulate the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) on the very pleasing and friendly way in which he has discharged the duties which devolved upon him. He has been frank and I think he has made the best of an impossible job.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Excise
maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF HON. J. A. ROBB, ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The job and the man are all right.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF HON. J. A. ROBB, ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I say that my hon. friend the Acting Minister of Finance has been frank. He has pointed out to us that in connection with a good many 'of the better showings that can be made, the activities of past years must be taken into consideration; he has been frank in showing that out of a debt reduction of $30,000,000 no less than $10,000,000 is due to the previous administration. He is frank also in pointing out that the surplus claimed is obtained by the elimination of obligations which we are now entering into, but absolutely real in view of the value of the investment and I call upon the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) for a corroboration of this-railway obligations to the extent of $/2,500,000, which we will finallv pay.
W hile my hon. friend has been brief in his statement, he has given us a lot of material which I think should be carefully considered, and I propose to move the adjournment of the debate, to which I think there is no objection, until Monday next, there being comparatively few members in attendance as a rule on Friday. Before submitting the motion I wish to point out one or two things that we on this side conceive should be looked into in connection with these budget propositions. The first thing that we look upon as essential in a budget at the present time is something which will enure to the benefit of Canada as a country rather than to the advantage of other nations; something which every patriotic Canadian will look upon as extremely necessary; something which would go far to stop the exodus of Canadian workingmen to the United States; something which will tend to change the present policy which however conceived will have for its inevitable result the expansion of the United States rather than the building up of Canada. That is one of the matters we shall give special attention to when studying these questions.
We also regard as essential the restoration of the purchasing power of the Canadian people as a whole. That is something which is of importance not only to the farming community but to every industry in the Dominion. We are wondering what is being done by this budget to check the exodus, and the admitted exodus, of 181,000 capable and educated Canadians, who paid their head tax and entered the United States. This startling disclosure is made by official returns. These men left Canada for the purpose of finding that work which was denied them in their own

The Budget-Sir Henry Drayton
country, that work which was denied them in the land of their birth. Now, we should like to find a policy adopted which would restore these 181,000 good Canadians to their native land and enable it to benefit from the resumption of their activities in the Dominion. Many of these men left Canada as a result of the closing down of our woollen factories. Many of them earned a livelihood of $29 a week; in mere labouring work others earned $23 a week. Reducing the amount lost to the low average earnings per capita of $1,000 a year one can see at a glance the great loss in the purchasing power of the Canadian home market on which at any rate the majority of our farmers depend. We have removed from that market a purchasing power of no less than $181,000,000, and we would expect something to be done in connection with the present budget to remedy that serious loss. We would further expect something to be done to help the Canadian farmer who to-day is shut out by an absolute barrier from his natural market to the south. Certainly the least we might expect is that something would be done to help him in his own market. Thus we would expect that the producer of cheese in Canada would have something done for him when we remember that the sales of American cheese in this Dominion have increased 86 per cent, while his own market has been cut in two. We would expect that something would be done for the great basic industry of agriculture, and especially for mixed farming the development of which my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) preaches so sedulously. We would expect something which would change the situation which permits American eggs to the amount of $2,416,000 to be sold in Canada, whereas the sale of Canadian eggs in the adjoining republic amounted to the small sum of only $49,000. We would also expect something to be done to help the vegetable grower of Canada whose market is encroached upon to a serious extent by products from the United States.
I do not know that we should expect impossibilities to be done by this budget,. That would be to restore to the industrial worker everywhere the confidence which he placed in the professions of faith of hon. gentlemen opposite in the Fielding-Laurier tariff which he desired. And at the same time the faith of the grain growers of the West that the Liberal platform of 1919 was seriously meant. Hon. gentlemen opposite have before them the task of reconciling these rival claims. We are going to consider the whole fiscal policy having regard to the doctrine preached by the Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding) last year that there
should be stability in tariff but stability looking to the expansion of all matters Canadian.
We have not the budget hefore us yet, but I want to make just one statement to the minister which is perhaps an answer to much that he has said in connection with traffic over our railways and the like, and that is simply this. There was a time when our railways in western territory were good assets, but we have got a return to-day by the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) showing how the earnings of the National system are made up. The hon. Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) talks about the great increase of industrial and agricultural activity that his measure will produce. Why, we have never had a bigger or better year, so far as volume is concerned, than the present year; and yet the whole earnings of all the western territories, the prairie provinces and British Columbia, for the last year amount to $72,000,000 and the operating expenses amount to $74,000,000; so that as a result, with the movement of the greatest crops we have ever had, we still have a railway deficit in actual operation in western Canada this yeai of $2,020,000. On the other hand, in Ontario and Quebec, in the central region of industry, the National Railways earn $127,900,000, with operating expenses of $109,212,000, a credit of $18,687,000. I hope a study of these resolutions that have been brought down will not result is this: That defenceless industrial Canada is further shackled, and that a complete Americanization of many lines of industry is made certain; that the exodus this year of 181,000 good working Canadians is to be indefinitely and permanently increased. We hope a study of these resolutions will not disclose these rasults. We fear it will, but we hope not. 1 beg to move the adjournment of the debate till next Monday.

I do not rise to oppose the resolution but I just want to bring certain facts to the attention of the minister. These people are situated in a peculiar country lying between two valleys. Their towns are located on the Canadian Pacific line, between Moose Jaw and Outlook, on the one hand, and on the Canadian National line on the other. Going west to the Canadian Pacific line they have to cross the Qu'Appelle valley, and to the east, going to the Canadian National line, they are obliged to cross the Squaw valley; and the nature of these valleys is such that these people must use four horses in order to market a two-horse load of grain. I have received many letters and telegrams with respect to this matter protesting against this line going from Dunblane crossing the river at Elbow and then going to Mawer if the intention is to reduce the chances of the inhabitants of this district of getting a line which will serve their requirements. I bring this matter to the attention of the minister so that he may place it before the railway board, because these people in their present 
circumstances are justly entitled to a railway through that district. Xf a railway went through the district it would provide considerable business for the Canadian National Railways which they are not enjoying to-day; and by reason of the character of that part of the country which I have mentioned it is of sufficient importance that the minister take a note of what I am saying and submit these representations to the board.

maintopic: RADVILLE-FIFE LAKE
speechtext:
The objection I have to this line is that it does not wholly serve the purposes for which our Canadian National branch lines are supposed to be built. The minister himself agrees with me in this statement and I have observed also that the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) takes the same view in statements he has made previously in this regard. In the building of these lines and in their location there should be taken into consideration not only the interests of the railways themselves but the desirability of serving the people who are already in the districts where railways are to be built. In order that I may state my objection clearly to this branch line as projected I shall explain the conditions that exist in that particular district. In 1904 or thereabouts the Canadian Northern built its main line from Winnipeg to Edmonton, cutting through the province of Saskatchewan, and about a year later there was built from that line a branch from Dauphin to the city of Prince Albert which, after swinging northward from Dauphin for about a hundred miles, then paralleled the existing line half way across the province of Saskatchewan. There was already at that time a line from Saskatoon to Prince Albert which later was acquired by the Canadian Northern Railway, thus enclosing a sort of rectangle. In this rectangle there was enclosed an area, roughly speaking, of 150 miles by 60 or 70 in width. That of course, it will be admitted, is too large a territory to be served by two lines, one on the south and the other on the north. Later on the Canadian Northern started to build a line cutting through that territory, but as this area was at that time sparsely settled, and as that company already encircled the territory with their own lines, very slow progress was made, and they did not reach Kelv-ington until about two years ago. For many years previous to that much of this territory had been settled very thickly. It is a good district. At the time the original railway was built, about 1904 or 1905, it was considerably wooded; but owing to the inroads of fires and the use of the wood by settlers the forest districts have been greatly reduced and much good land has been brought under cultivation; in fact the whole territory may be said to be fairly well settled to-day. The other line which was started by the Canadian Northern, and eventually became the Canadian National line from Swan River to Kel-vington-or what was always known as the Thunder Hill extension-did not break this territory into two by any means. It ran practically parallel to the Winnipeg-Edmon-ton line of the Canadian National Railway,
and about twenty miles from it, leaving a territory north of that line to the Dauphin-Prince Albert line averaging from sixty to seventy miles in width. As I have already stated, this territory has become settled and cultivated, and a vast amount of grain is taken out annually. At the same time the country to the northward has become a heavy producing area, and there are millions of bushels of grain to be drawn out of there every year. This line in its original form, as presented last year, was shown as a cutoff from the Swan River-Prince Albert line across to Kelvington. It would have served the territory and would have been very advantageous to the settlers who went in there many years ago anticipating railroad accommodation.
When the Soldier Settlement Board was re-establishing the soldiers who were placed under its care, this very choice land no doubt appealed to its officials as being admirably suited for such settlement, and a very large soldier settlement was located in the area around Kelvington and immediately north-Perigord, Nobleville, Pre Ste. Marie, Bjorkdale and Speddington. The soldiers took up their land with the definite understanding that a branch of the Canadian National Railways, which had been projected before that time, would be built to serve them. They have broken up perhaps more than half of their land. I was in there last fall and was surprised at the way in which they had advanced themselves, being so distant from railway facilities. They have good land and have made themselves homes there. Now this resolution would carry the branch in a westerly direction to connect with a branch of the Canadian Pacific, and would not serve those settlers.
The fact is that last year the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, realizing that they had an advantage when the Canadian National board was not allowed to build, constructed their line from a point south running generally northerly through this district, but without serving the areas that I have mentioned where the soldier settlers are located. The Canadian Pacific had a definite objective to the north, and naturally they wanted to reach it by the shortest route. To do so they built through very rough territory [DOT]-scrub land and forest area-about fifteen miles away from the soldier settlement. In order to reach the Canadian Pacific line these soldier settlers will have to build fifteen or twenty miles of road.
I maintain, Mr. Chairman, that it is not good policy in this case to build thirteen miles of railway to reach a Canadian Pacific
C.N.R.-Branch Lines

branch line and then secure running rights over it, as I understand the intention to be. I submit it would be far better to build this branch through the soldier settlement, for in doing so it would not be necessary to closely parallel the Canadian Pacific. The resolution itself shows that the route is thirteen miles away from the Canadian Pacific, and it would not be necessary to build closer to the competing line to reach the northern branch toward which this line was projected last year. By turning north from Kelvington rather than westerly, as the resolution calls for, I am quite certain that a route could be found through the territory in which the soldiers are settled. Not only would it then serve these settlers, but it would also serve the purpose intended last year-at least, one of the arguments offered in support of the line at that time was that it would make the necessary cut-off for the Prince Albert and Melfort country. There is an enormous quantity of grain being produced in that country to-day, and the Dauphin-Prince Albert line is not capable of carrying the freight trains necessary to take that grain out. One of the engineers told me last year that in his estimation it would cost as much to put that road into shape for such traffic as it would to build this cut-off, for heavier steel would would have to be laid and the whole road practically re-constructed, with the exception of the grade.
I know the argument will be advanced that by connecting with the Canadian Pacific branch, as the Canadian Pacific intend eventually to cross the Prince Albert branch, running rights can be secured over it and accommodation afforded in that way. But I submit that this is not good policy, and that where settlement is in dire need of railway service, and where eventually the Canadian National will have to build their line to afford adequate service, it is false economy at this time to build thirteen miles to reach'* the Canadian Pacific, when that mileage would be one-fifth of the whole construction required to reach their own line to the northward, and would in itself be that much closer to the soldier settlement when built.
The freight from this territory is not merely prospective; it is there to offer at the present time. Two years ago when the Thunder Hill branch of the Canadian National, of which this project is an extension, reached Kelvington, about 750,000 bushels of grain was carried out the first fall after steel was laid down. Kelvington is only twenty-five miles south of these soldier settlements, and there will be immense quantities of grain to be taken out if this line is carried through.

Let me show the other side of the argument as it affects those people. I am quite safe in saying that on an average they are fifteen miles away from the Canadian Pacific which is projected but not yet built, and they will have to build through the very worst kind of country, intersected by lakes and creeks, and the Barrier river and the Red Deer river will have to be bridged. It will make it almost prohibitive for these new municipalities to undertake such expensive road construction.
I know that the privileges that a private member has in amending a resolution such as this are somewhat limited, and it is much against my will that I would move to amend it at all. The building of thirteen miles into this territory would be of very little help, but I want to point out-and this statement was made by a Canadian National engineer who went over the territory during the last four or five months-that along the line of the route I have intimated it should follow, and the one that it was originally intended to follow, there are 666 farmers established. If this line is extended westwardly in the direction that this resolution proposes it should go, a good number of those 666 farmers will not be there this time next year. They will give up all hope of getting railway facilities if they are to have no railroad any closer to them than the Canadian Pacific branch, which is under construction but not yet completed, and which, as I have pointed out, is almost inaccessible to them. If this 13 miles of line is built in a northerly direction it will at least have the effect of holding these people to their land and their homes; they will go on, I have no doubt, working as they have done for years past in the expectation that they will eventually get relief so far as railway facilities are concerned. With these considerations in mind, therefore, I beg to move, seconded by the member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell), that resolution No. 12 be amended by striking out the words "in a westerly direction, to a point in township 37, range 13, west of . the 2nd meridian," and substituting therefor the words "in a northerly direction, east of Nut Lake."

speechtext:
I know the territory to which the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Stewart) has been referring and I know the need for service there. I have been through that district and I know that the people are looking forward to some railway connection. maintopic: RADVILLE-FIFE LAKE
speechtext:
I wish to associate myself with what has been said by the
5 p.m. hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Stewart regarding the necessity for railway facilities for the settlers in this district. If anything were necessary to prove the productiveness of that section it is proved by the fact that almost immediately after the defeat of the Branch Lines Bill in the Senate last year the Canadian Pacific built through almost the same territory that the bill had intended to cover. The hon. member for St-Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler) complained about the building of railways through sparsely settled districts, and I agree with him. But when settlerrs are already in a certain district, placed there, as they were in most cases, by agents of the Dominion government, the Soldier Settlement Board, there is a distinct obligation on the part of the government to provide them with the necessary facilities. A few evenings ago we had a discussion in this House regarding a vote of $600,000 for the completion of the tower on this building. It seems to me that an attempt was made on that occasion to put those who were opposing that vote in a false position by raising the question of the memorial, chamber which is to be provided in the tower. I submit that the best memorial we could erect to our dead soldiers would be to look after the living. These men who have gone in there, who were located there by the Soldier Settlement Board, are in such a position that they must lose everything, they must give up and leave, if they are not provided with proper transportation facilities.
Regarding the whole question of branch lines and the adverse comments we have heard in this House, it seems to me that

C.N.R.-Branch Lines

many hon. members who have spoken on the subject have not been fair to western Canada. A few years ago when a railway company came before parliament and asked for a charter to build a branch line or an extension of a main line it was considered a distinct favour to them to grant them a charter. Now, Sir, we have hon. members complaining that railway construction is being authorized, it looks as if some hon. members were viewing railway construction from a different angle altogether. Some hon. members from eastern Canada, particularly the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. Denis) and one of the Toronto members, tried to make it appear that the construction of these branch lines was a direct bonus to western Canada. Sir, I can hardly permit their statements to go unchallenged and I would therefore take the liberty of quoting a few figures to show how unfounded they are. The hon. member for Joliette, who I regret is not in his seat, made this rather significant statement:
These lines by the very nature of things must come out of the moneys of the country and must increase the deficits, and the province of Quebec is paying for them.
I submit that is not a very fair statement to make. About $225,000,000 of the public money of this country has been spent on the canal system the use of which is granted free of charge to vessels traversing those waters. Then, many millions of dollars have been spent on our rivers and harbours. This expenditure also is a direct bonus to the people who use these facilities. They are of very little benefit to the people of western Canada. Again, in reference to the railways I maintain that we in the West have been paying an unfair proportion of the railway charges in the past. The hon. members to whom I have referred seem to argue that the greatest amount of the railway deficits has accrued in western Canada. The actual facts demonstrate that in good crop years, when we have a bountiful harvest in western Canada, the earnings of the railways show a remarkable increase and a corresponding decrease in deficits. By referring to the decision of the Board of Railway Commissioners in the western rates ease we find an admission on the part. of the commissioners that discrimination existed in freight rates against western Canada; They admitted frankly that western Canada was being charged a higher freight rate than eastern Canada and they justified it on the grounds that in eastern Canada there was competition of American roads and the water competition on the lakes. I should like to quote a few figures in sub-

stantiation of this statement; they are taken from statements placed before the Railway Commission by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. Dealing with the five-year period from 1907 to 1911 the Canadian Pacific show an operating ratio-that is the amount spent that was necessary to earn a dollar-in eastern Canada, that is east of Fort William, of 72 cents, on the prairie section of 56 cents, and on the western section, that is British Columbia, 60 cents. The net earnings for this period were: In the western section-that is the prairies and British Columbia, $91,500,000, and in the eastern section, $43,500,000. That is, after deducting all operating expenses, the western roads showed $48,000,000 more profit than the eastern section. For the five-year period from 1912 to 1916 the eastern section shows an operating revenue of $226,500,000, and the western section $356,500,000. The operating ratio for this period in the eastern section was 73.3, for the prairie section 54.5, and for the western section 57 cents. The net earnings for the same period were-in the eastern section $60,000,000, and in the western section $152,500,000. Then we have the period from 1916 to 1920. During that period the operating ratio in the eastern section was 80-95, and in the western section 67-30. For the year 1921 the operating revenue on the eastern section was $85,500,000, and on the western section $101,900,000, The operating ratio for that year in the eastern section was 77-21, and in the western section 70-54. The net earnings on the eastern section amounted to $11,000,000, and on the western section to $30,000,000.
Now, Sir, if we summarize the figures for this whole period we find that in the fifteen years from 1907 to 1921 the net earnings in the western section of the Canadian Pacific Railway were $405,000,000, and in the eastern section $177,000,000. These figures almost prove the contention sometimes made "that the western section has paid for the Canadian Pacific but the country does not own it." I may say that in these quotations the western figures include also the British Columbia section. This is unfair to the prairie provinces because the cost of operating is much higher in the British Columbia section than it is in the prairies.
The charge has frequently been made that grain was carried at a much lower rate than other commodities, and the attempt has even been made to prove that a bonus was granted to the western farmers in the matter of the handling of grain. Now, Sir, if we analyse the earnings for the different months we find that the railways have always made the great-

C.N.R___Branch Lines
est profit during the months in which the grain was being handled. For instance, we find that in the year 1920 the operating ratio on the Canadian Pacific Railway during the month of August was 80.23, that is it cost 80.23 to earn a dollar. In the month of October when the heavy movement of grain was on it cost them only 56.46 to earn a dollar; and in the month of November of the same year the operating ratio was only 66.32. In the year 1921 the operating ratio in the month of October was only 55.02 cents. In the month of November, 1921, the net revenue on the eastern section was only $4,403, and the operating ratio 99.23. Now, Sir, in the same month the net revenue on the western section was $5,048,000. In the month of December, 1921, the eastern section showed a net revenue of $566,000, and the western section a net revenue of $3,170,000. The year 1920 showed an operating ratio of 84.70 on the Canadian Pacific Railway, but in 1921 it had dropped to 82.28, and in 1922 it had fallen to 80.55.
Now, Sir, when the Crowsnest pass rate agreement was being considered by the special Railway committee of this House the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company made the prediction that if the Crowsnest rates were permitted to go into effect his company would be unable to pay its fixed charges and dividends. And yet after the Canadian Pacific had handled the most of that crop at the beginning of the new year we find the president of the company sending a message to his men in which he said:
The new year opens under auspices more favourable than any since the conclusion of the war.
This was in strange contrast with the pessimistic prediction in which he indulged when the rate question was being considered by the Railway committee. I should like hon. members to note that in the year 1922, the year in which the Crowsnest rates came into effect, the operating ratio of the Canadian Pacific dropped from 82.28 to 80.55. Analysing the amounts of grain handled in previous years we find that a low operating ratio was coincident with large crops. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company handled 4,349,000 tons of grain in 1920 and in that year their operating ratio was 84.70. In 1921, they handled 4,812,000 tons and the operating ratio was 82.28. In the year 1922 they handled 6,888,000 tons of grain and the operating ratio dropped to 80.55.	'

speechtext:
With regard to the
amendment, the practice is altogether against moving an amendment to preliminary resolutions preceding money bills. These resolutions have the recommendation of the Crown, and the recommendation of the Crown is signified. They are preliminary to the bill being introduced and referred to the committee, where any hon. member may move amendments which do not increase the impost or amount to be expended. In view of these resolutions and the variation proposed involving the construction of the new branch line which this amendment would really authorize, I think the amendment is out of order. Rule No. 77 reads:
If any motion be made in the House for any public aid or charge upon the people, the consideration and debate thereof may not be presently entered upon,

C.N.R-Branch Lines
but shall be adjourned till such further day as the House thinks fit to appoint; and then it shall be referred to a committee of the whole House before any resolution or vote of the House do pass thereupon.
Then I refer to May, page 457:
In like manner, after the question has been proposed on an amendment, and it has appeared that the amendment would vary the incidence of taxation, or increase the charge upon the consolidated fund, the Speaker has declined to put the question.
I feel that I should follow that rule. The ground is that an amendment to a resolution is varying the incidence of taxation and may increase the amount of expenditure. The hon. member is not prevented from moving during various stages of the bill, or when the bill goes into committee, any amendments he desires, with those limitations. I feel that this amendment at this time is out of order.

maintopic: RADVILLE-FIFE LAKE

I wish to say a word with
regard to this line. It has been looked forward to for a great many years by the people who went in there and it is on behalf of the returned men that I wish to speak because
[The Chairman. [
they went in there on the distinct understanding that this line was as good as built. Cost
Acadia Valley, Mile 0-42

This branch runs through a good agricultural district with a considerable percentage of the land cultivated. Like other areas in this district, it is subject to short crops in dry seasons, but in seasons of sufficient precipitation will produce a heavy yield of wheat per acre.
The justification for completing this line is that about $274,500, or more than one-quarter of the money

With this line completed the farmers would save on the average 10 miles road haul, and computing this as worth to i'hem three-quarters of a cent per bushel, per mile hauled, on the 1,000,000 bushels estimated to come off this branch, there would be saved to the farmers each year $75,000 on grain alone. speechtext:
I think it is important
that the resolution should be discussed. While there has been some question as to the eastern terminus of the branch, it is of considerable importance in a way in that it affects the Canadian National Railways in a respect in which many of the other branch lines do not. It is estimated that this branch will cost $3,700,000 for 115 miles. To-day there are millions of bushels of grain being hauled across the international boundary line and marketed at United States points, and that 'entire business is lost to Canada. We hear much talk to-day about patronising home industries, but here is a place where the business of thousands of our people, who to all intents and purposes are American citizens, is lost to Canada. They have produced in that country between three million and four million bushels of grain this year and the bulk of it is going via an American route. It is not as though it were taking trade away from some other Canadian road if we build this branch such as the Canadian Pacific Railway. It is taking it from an American road, and I say that it is sound national economy to build this line immediately. That country has been settled for about fifteen years, many of the inhabitants having gone in there on the strength of the promise, implied at least, that a road would be built soon. They are a very fine class of settlers and their great want to-day is a railway. At the present time there are many farmers who are not working their land over 25 per cent capacity and they cannot afford to develop a greater area than they have under cultivation, while they have to haul grain distances ranging between 25 and 45 miles. The people are simply stalling, waiting for a railroad; indeed, many of them are not working the land at all, but are just letting it lie idle. They are so far from any railway that, of course, there is not much encumbrance against them, for the reason that they could not borrow money. But they are an industrious class of people and if they were assured that a line would be built soon they would immediately get busy and would produce wealth whereby the country would be richer. The Dominion of Canada would be enriched, not by the net amount, but by the gross wealth produced by these people. While I do not want to differ from the engineers in regard to the route, no doubt we should be largely guided by them as to where it should go. The latest proposal is that it

C.N.R.-Branch Lines
should run 20 miles south of Radville and then westerly about 10 to 15 miles north of the boundary. I am anxious to see this work undertaken at the earliest possible moment in the interests not only of the settlers themselves but of the country at large.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: RADVILLE-FIFE LAKE
speechtext:
We might as well
deal with this matter now if the minister (Mr. Graham) is agreeable. I have had some correspondence and telegrams on this subject and I had an invitation to go and examine the country last fall. I did so and I think that my hon. friend (Mr. Morrison) has described the situation pretty much as it is. I have here a telegram with respect to the route from the Hon. C. M. Hamilton, Minister of Agriculture for Saskatchewan, and an ex-director of the Canadian National Railways. Mr. Hamilton is familiar with the whole question and he knows the territory concerned quite well. His telegram, addressed to myself, reads:
Construction during present year at least one hundred and twenty-five miles Radville-Fife lake proposed branch Canadian National Railways urgent. Absolutely impossible haul wheat and other farm produce thirty-five to fifty miles. Settlers almost discouraged; numbers have left territory, others holding on hoping for relief. Proposed extension from Bengough-Fife lake serves only small portion of territory and leaves district so divided it cannot possibly have adequate railway accommodation for many years.
Unless one is fairly familiar with the territory he will not appreciate the significance of the statement I have just quoted. The road from Bengough to Fife Lake does not serve the entire territory; whereas the proposed line serves about twice the area, and fully 80 per cent of the particular district that would have been served by the other line. The proposed route is very much preferable because it serves the entire country parallel to the international boundary for a distance of 115 miles and not only takes care of the freight and the tonnage generally of the settlers along that line but prevents their transference across the boundary into the United States. This emigration has been going on in that part of the country for some eight or ten years and conditions have become so bad in some districts that the settlers have largely left. The territory is a splendid one, and while it is true that a small portion of it for about 15 miles east and west is rough and undulating, and therefore adapted mainly^ to grazing, the country on the whole, particularly in the west, is one of the finest plains that one could wish to look upon. If this line is gone on with it does not deprive the people west of Bengough of the hope that some day the Bengough line will be extended to Willow Bunch. That may not be done to-morrow, but there is no reason why at some subsequent time, when railway bills are being again introduced into the House, steps may not be taken to have that line built. In the meantime, I would point out that the Radville line passes through a territory in which many of the settlers have been tried as by fire and are still carrying on despite the discouragement which they have experienced. Many of them are growing from five thousand to ten thousand bushels of wheat in addition to flax and coarse grains, besides raising cattle and other produce. This line is urgently required and my only regret is that some of it will not be constructed this year. The Premier of Saskatchewan is anxious to see the road built, as is everyone else who is familiar with the circumstances; and as all persons will be reasonably well supplied it is important that the work should be proceeded with. If this is done, then later on, when settlement and tonnage both increase, the road from Bengough to Willow Bunch might be undertaken. Meanwhile the people have got together and discussed the whole situation. Provincial members and local councils have formed what is known as a railway committee and they have threshed the question out from every possible angle. I have a communication from Mr. George Spence, one of the representatives of the south country, in which he gives me a summary of the con-elusions arrived at, which is in the direction I have indicated, the important point being that the line from Radville to Fife Lake should be constructed as the best solution for the trouble that has existed for so many years. I was not through that country in the early years but I was there last year and I am familiar with the entire district. I was familiar with the work that was undertaken under the provincial guarantees and as I was in the Saskatchewan government at that time I know of the deadlock that occurred. I am glad to inform the House that that deadlock seems now to be capable of solution by means of this particular line, and as nearly as is humanly possible this line will meet the most urgent requirements of the people, whereas the other one would not. I have no hesitation, from my own personal knowledge of the situation and from the representations that I have received from public men and municipal councils, in saying that the line in question will serve a very large proportion of territory which has been in dire need of railway accommodation for many years, so much so, that sick at heart, many of them have already left. I
C.N.R.-Branch Lines

have correspondence from many who went to the United States telling me that they are ready to come back just as soon as this line is constructed.

maintopic: RADVILLE-FIFE LAKE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, on account of certain natural barriers no one road would be capable of serving the whole area between the present Canadian Pacific line and the international boundary, a distance of about forty miles. Therefore for some years there has been a dispute amongst the settlers as to the location of a branch line. An understanding has been reached between the Canadian National authorities and the Canadian Pacific under which this area is treated as Canadian National territory. Last year a line was proposed from Bengough to Fife Lake, but the bill was killed in the Senate, as we know, I was never in that country until last fall. Leaving the railway I drove forty miles to the international border. In the course of the afternoon I met over two hundred teams loaded with grain, on their way to the railroad. I spoke to some of the drivers and found they had come all the way up to fifty miles, and that it took them from two to four days to make the round trip. They told me the country was splendid and that their crops ran from twenty-five to forty bushels to the acre. As I got nearer to the boundary line I found the people were too far away from our railways to ship their grain and had to take it over to the American railway lines. I understand that a million and a half bushels of Canadian wheat from this section goes over the Amercian railways in the average year, making a profit for this line and adding to the trade and commerce of the neighbouring republic.
I was surprised at the state of development. I expected to see all the characteristics of a pioneer country, but I found every evidence of well-established settlement. We judge a country by the condition of the farms and buildings. I saw well cultivated farms, well constructed buildings and, above all, fine schools. I went into three or four of the schools along the border and spoke to the teachers and pupils, and I found they were up to date in their educational methods. I talked to boys and girls ranging from ten to fourteen years of age, and they told me they had never seen a store nor a town of any kind, the parents not being able to give them a trip of eighty or ninety miles to the nearest urban centre. I sent a message by the children to the parents that I only hoped the children would live long enough to get some of the railroad advantages which their fathers and mothers had been deprived of all these years.

Now, this railway is in a different position from the other branches which we have been discussing. Hon. members have said, "We must scrutinize every dollar of expenditure at this particular time in the history of Canada." And rightly so. It is the duty of parliament to scrutinize every expenditure. But I am going to give the committee an agreeable surprise-this money does not have to be expended by the federal parliament; it has been already provided. That is one of the particular reasons why I got on my feet; the other is to give you the best authority for the building of this branch that we have in the province of Saskatchewan. I will show hon. members where the money is coming from, I am about to quote from the Regina Standard of a recent date, and I may say that the bill referred to has since become law. This is the quotation:
Authority for the provincial treasury to release certain money for the construction of Canadian National branch lines is sought in an Act which was given second reading in the legislature last night.
Premier Dunning intimated to the house that subject to agreement being reached with the Canadian National authorities the government had a preference for the money being used towards the construction of a portion at least of the Bengough extension in the south-
That is the territory we are speaking of.
-and the Turtleford-Hafford branch in the north of the province.
" We regard those two as being the most needed in the province at present," he said, " but it may not be possible to work out an agreement with the railway company and my remarks on this matter must not be taken as definite promise that these lines will be built."
Premier Dunning explained that years ago when the province guaranteed the bonds of the railway companies the system in operation was that the railway companies had authority to sell bonds guaranteed by the province, but they had no authority to use the proceeds which were deposited in a bank to the credit of the provincial treasurer. Then as the railways were constructed the money was to be released by the provincial treasurer at rates per mile set out in the original Act.
The Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Northern ceased operating as separate entities some time ago and during his experience as provincial treasurer for the last eight years it had been impossible to release the money. A sum of $1,202,825.24 had been standing to the credit of the treasury in connection with this fund for a number of years. Repeated efforts had been made by the companies to obtain release of the money but the treasury had been unable to satisfy itself that the railways had been built. The province had not lost anything as the bank interest on the money had been paid to the railway company and it had paid the interest on the bonds.
There is no question that a large part of the money for the building of this road can be secured from the provincial government.
I have just one further word to say on behalf of the people in that south country. I have no axe to grind because there is not one

C.N.R.-Branch Lines
chance in a thousand that I will ever represent those people again-the Redistribution Bill will look after that. They are a loyal energetic and resourceful people; if they were not they would not have endured so many disadvantages and hardships all these years. But "hope deferred maketh the heart sick," and if the people of Canada want to retain in their midst some of the best settlers they have to-day, something must be done very quickly to secure them the railroad accommodation which they are entitled to, for their patience has almost ceased to be a virtue.

Mr. Chairman, in view of the moving statement by my hon. friend from Moose Jaw (Mr. Hopkins) perhaps the resolution can go through, subject to this understanding, that some facts be furnished about the branch line. There is no question that some railways ought to be built in this section, and I am not opposing proper railway construction there. In fact I have already agreed to a great deal. I hope the next time we agree to these things we shall not be told that we are dealing with a Conservative constituency and that that is the reason for the agreement. A very careful survey of costs should therefore be made. As the whole matter will subsquently be gone into and these phases of it can be considered again, I have no objection to the resolutions being reported.

Will the minister give us a little information regarding this item?
Hon. CHARLES A. STEWART (Minister of the Interior): The Board of Examiners for Dominion land surveyors is organised under the provision of section 9 of the Dominion Land Surveys Act. It consists of the Surveyor General and of two Dominion topographical surveyors. The present members are Dr. Deville, Harry B. Parry, and W. M. Tobey. Dr. Klotz was a member of the board, but he is deceased and there has been an appointment since.
The regular annual meeting of the board is in February. Another meeting is usually held in May for the convenience of students in engineering who have just graduated at the university. There are four different examinations, viz:- the examination for admission as an articled pupil, the full and the limited examination for admission as land surveyor and the examination for certificate as Dominion topographical surveyor. The questions for each examination are prepared by the members of the board and the answers of the candidates are read and marked by these three members. The questions being mostly mathematical and scientific, all the possible solutions of each problem have to be worked out by the examiners. The preparation and reading of the papers involve a large amount of work. The surveyor general, Dr. Klotz and W. M. Tobey had no time to spare during office hours, so that most of the work for the board had to be done at night.
The fee for the members of the board and of their substitutes is fixed by the Dominion Land Surveys Act at $7.50 per day. The fee of the secretary and of the sub-examiners is fixed at $5 per day.
The amount asked is to cover the fees of the members of the board or their substitutes, the fees of the sub-examiners and secretary, the printing of the questions, blank forms, etc., stationery, rent of rooms and furniture for holding examinations, and the travelling expenses of the examiners who are not permanent officials of the inside service.

speechtext:
Under this item, I presume the veiy important question of reforestation and conservation of our forests generally

Supply-Interior
would properly come. I personally do not purpose discussing the question at length, but I should like the minister to give to the committee some idea of what has been done within the knowledge of and actually by the officials of this department towards proper conservation. I feel a little alarmed at the very rapid depletion of our forests. In many districts these forests are being cut and manufactured into timber, without any effort whatever being made at reforestation; nor, so far as I am able to see, is very much being done in the way of intelligent conservation of the forests that we have. Losses by fire and so on are really appalling. It is true that our forest wealth is extensive; that we are inclined to look on the supply as illimitable; but, as a matter of fact, I think most students of the subject agree that exhaustion of our forest wealth is really well within sight. Whether the government is doing anything at all in the matter would be of interest to the committee, and if the minister could give us some information along that line, it would be of value.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: I should be glad to devote a few minutes to this question of forestry, and the time of the committee might be well spent in discussing it. It is one of the most important questions with which we have to deal in the Department of the Interior. Perhaps I can bring the matter home to members of the committee much better by a statement in round figures of the quantity of timber that is manufactured in Canada annually. All the cordwood, the piles, the ties, and all other timber, including pulp-wood, manufactured and unmanufactured, amount annually in Canada to almost twelve billion feet. And the next startling statement I have to make is this, that we destroy about one billion feet more annually than we manufacture. I make that statement in order to bring as forcibly as possible to the attention of the committee the terrific waste which is going on in connection with the forest wealth of Canada.
