speechtext: The minister has referred to certain forest losses. Are these losses all due to fires?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
well as the Dominion land block in the northern portion of that province; and over that particular area we exercise a special control. We have not been so unfortunate with respect to fire as they have been in some of the provinces in which the various governments control their own timber; but in any case we must take more drastic steps to prevent destruction by fire from any cause. With that end in view I have sought by way of convention to bring together the forestry officials of the various provinces and those of the federal government. We have had some very interesting discussions at our recent convention. Just prior to the opening of parliament we had a gathering at which all the provinces were represented and we discussed these subjects for five or six days, trying to co-ordinate our views and to learn from one another *what efforts we have been putting forth for the suppression of fire, for the purpose of adopting more stringent and more effective measures' for fire control. At the very outset it would take an army of men adequately to control the fire situation. True, we have fire ranging forces in all the provinces. They are employed by the federal government for a period of six months in the prairies, and they patrol the forests for the purpose of keeping down and preventing fires. We have been fairly successful in that respect and I believe that year by year we are making more headway. We propose to utilize in this service the flying corps of the Department of National Defence. An aeroplane will cover very much more territory than a man in a canoe, and the vision is much more extended, as one may readily understand, than would be the case with a tower or the ordinary patrol through the waterways in the forests. We hope in this way to accomplish much better results than have been obtained in the past. If we can detect a fire in the incipient stages we can put it out with the help of one or two men, whereas, if it has been burning for a week, it requires perhaps two or three hundred. We have adopted more radical measures in all the provinces, and this has been the result of our convention. We have discussed various methods and considered the efficiency of power pumps particularly, and each province will now display renewed interest in fire suppression work. I dwell upon this point because I think it is the most important gnd the one in regard to which we should make the greatest strides towards securing a proper solution.
I was pleased to note the other day that the province of Ontario had purchased ten or twelve aeroplanes which they intend to use in the northern part of the province this year.

And the province of Quebec, I think, will do the same. Our flying will of course be confined largely to the three prairie provinces and to some extent in British Columbia. In order that we might place the matter before the public with a greater degree of force, if that is possible, this convention suggested the adoption of what will be known as fire prevention week beginning with the 27th day of this month. All the provinces are joining and we are spending $5,000 in propaganda, writing to all the banks and all the newspapers in an endeavour to interest them in the matter, so that we may get the seriousness of the whole thing impressed upon the people in a more vivid way than ever before, and emphasize the necessity for everyone to exercise due care throughout the season in which the fire hazard prevails. I hope that it will cut the destruction by fire in half within at least two years, and that in three or four years the loss will be reduced to the absolute minimum. I do not believe we shall ever be able to remove the fire hazard entirely, for even in our cities and towns there is a very heavy annual loss by fire notwithstanding the very efficient firefighting appliances in use. The amazing feature is that the appalling loss both in our fo'ests and our urban centres is very largely the result of carelessness. If we could only educate the people to be careful in this regard we would accomplish a very great deal in preventing fire losses everywhere. We are dependent to a great extent on our educational propaganda. We are asking for an increased amount for inspectional work in the western provinces. There, of course, the forests are strictly the property of the federal government. But I do not lay very much stress on this circumstance because I realize that our forest wealth is of vital importance to the whole Dominion. The number of men employed in labouring work alone in connection with the manufacture of forest products is very large, and the capital invested runs into many millions of dollars. Our aim should be to replenish annually a little more than we cut off our timber lands. That is what I am asking the Forestry branch-of the Department of the Interior to attempt, and I think every forestry man in the employ of the provinces is anxious to accomplish the same end.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: (York): Do you mean depletion both from cutting and from destruction by fire?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I mean we should aim to reproduce, if you will, the same

Supply-Interior
amount of timber as is manufactured each year, so that we may have this perpetual source of wealth for the people.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: To what extent is reforestation taking place? The statement has been published that the amount of timber reproduced in this way would last our mills just six days.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Yes, but I do not pin my faith entirely on tree-planting. What struck our visitors from all the Dominions and Great Britain when they attended our forestry convention was that owing to climatic and soil conditions in Canada reproduction goes on without the necessity of our incurring the expense of tree-planting to any considerable extent. Indeed, I think I am safe in asserting that if we increased our annual cut to more than fifteen billion feet, by the prevention of fire losses there would be reproduced by nature an*equivalent amount each year. But I think our forest wealth is so important that we should not stop at eliminating the fire hazard,-every destructive influence should receive our very earnest attention.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Is there any danger from fire to young trees if all slash and rubbish are removed?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Of course,
one could speak all evening about forestry methods. Therein lies part of our difficulty to-day and the reason why we must have a uniform system of logging regulations. Each of the provinces is in competition in the timber market, and if you place restrictions upon logging in one province that do not apply in the other provinces, there is of course a benefit to the loggers who are free from restrictions. So if we are to have any success in our attempts to reduce the fire hazard to a minimum there must be co-ordination in this direction and the provinces must co-operate with the Dominion.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Has the minister come to any definite arrangements as to uniform slashing and other regulations?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
We have
made considerable headway in that direction. There is a difficulty in the province of British Columbia, where licenses have been granted under certain terms. But there is the greatest amount of interest in evidence by the forestry officials themselves to reach a uniform basis with respect to uniform regulations to reduce the fire hazard due from logging operations.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Outside of interest, what actually has been agreed upon?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
My hon.
friend well knows that the slash disposal regulations of the Department of the Interior are much more rigorous than those in vogue in the provinces. The provincial authorities have expressed their willingness to adopt our regulations; the only exception is British Columbia. There the Forestry department have doubts as to whether or not slash disposal could be taken care of on account of the very large amount that accumulates as the result of logging operations in the province. They say it would be very expensive to deal with it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Have any of the provinces actually adopted those regulations? If so, are the regulations applicable to leaseholders now in operation and contracts now under way, or merely to future leaseholders and future contracts?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: That practical difficulty exists with respect to present leaseholders. But the regulations are to be embodied, I think almost without exception, in all new leases.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: That will not get us very far.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
My hon.
friend will understand that we cannot drive; we can only encourage and coax.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: We cannot drive in the provincial domain; but undoubtedly the provinces would have power to make the new regulations apply to existing leases, and unless the minister succeeds in inducing them to do so he will not get very far.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
These
changes cannot be made in a day. I confess it is slow work getting the public to understand the value of our forest resources and how rapidly we are depleting them. But a very strong interest is in evidence among all forestry officials who have had to do with the conservation of our forest wealth. If we can arouse our provinces to action, I think they would make proper logging methods retroactive in so far as leaseholders are concerned. At least, that is my hope.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
With regard to the disposal of the tops and the refuse after logging in Alberta, I do not know the facts, but I think there is a feeling that the department in asking the loggers to dispose of that material are holding the leaseholders responsible for any fire that may occur. Is there any more responsibility on those holding leases than upon persons who travel through the woods?
Supply-Interior

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: The leaseholders have to pay half the cost if a fire occurs. But what they are complaining about is not that so much as the provisions with respect to the disposal of slash, in comparison with those applicable to operators in any one of the provinces. But if we are somewhat arbitrary in dealing with the people operating on Crown lands, we are setting an example which the other provinces might follow.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: What has been the experience as to the practicability of the method the minister has been describing? Has it actually been possible to carry it out?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Oh yes;
you can carry out any regulation, although you may have a little difficulty in doing so. We have to enforce that.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The disposal of that slash
is one of the most difficult problems we have.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Slash, of
course, is responsible for a great fire hazard. The forest wealth of Canada is so important -and I think in the future we will realize this-that if we forced them to cut up every top and burn it, even green, it would be worth while. It might be expensive, but it would be in the interests of the preservation of our forest wealth. That is my candid opinion in the matter. I have absolutely no sympathy with any attempt to avoid the regulations with respect to slash disposal.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Can you not
make the leaseholder take that view as well as the government? Could he be made to see that it is in his interests to operate with due regard to the maintenance of the timber wealth?

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: How does the government dispose of the timber on burned over areas which have not been previously under lease?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: If it is in the prairie provinces, where we control, we immediately put the burned area up for sale and the timber is salvaged.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Is it not true that in many cases or in all cases the timber on burned over areas is sold at a very small proportion of the price which it would bring if it were green?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: One half the dues under permit is what we have to sell it for.	.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The stumpage also is
lower?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Oh, yes.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Does the minister not consider that in many cases there is a very strong incentive in that to set out fires?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: We have a suspicion that that happens once in a while, particularly where there is an area of, say two or three sections, a small area that can be conveniently burned. But we have pretty rigid regulations, and although we may not catch every offender it is getting more difficult all the time to do that sort of thing.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Has the department any fire marshal or other official who investigates these fires and ascertains the cause?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Yes, every case is followed up.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: I suppose if there is a suspicion with regard to a certain party he would not get the benefit of the reduction?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Well, we try to get conviction if we can catch him, that is all.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Would the minister give us some idea of the terms of the leases? Are they issued for a term of years with conditions which obtain throughout that term, or has the department the right to vary the conditions from year to year? I am not quite as familiar with the West as I am with Ontario. Do these leases merely cover the railway belt, or what part? In British Columbia I suppose they are confined to the railway belt.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: As to the timber over which the Dominion government have control, there is provision for cancellation at the end of each year if it is desired.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That is exactly as it is in
Ontario. The regulations, then, are absolutely in the hands of the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Yes, we can make any changes we desire, any
9 p.m. regulations from time to time.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Then what was said to my
leader a moment ago would hardly be correct.
I understood the minister to say you could not drive, you could not force; as I understand it, these leases are issued with the right to cancellation at the end of any year, so that in issuing new licenses you can impose your own terms.

Supply-Interior

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: What I spoke of in reply to the leader of the opposition was the leases in the provinces, not the timber controlled by the federal government. The federal government have regulations for the disposal of slash which would make it extremely difficult for many of the old leaseholders. As my hon. friend knows, in Ontario, in Quebec, and in British Columbia outside the railway belt, the provincial governments themselves own and control the natural resources and make their own regulations. The difficulty that arises there is that in many cases the provisions of the lease cover the period during which the timber is cut off, and I presume that it would be difficult to change these definite provisions- But in all the new leases rigid control is provided for, and there is provision whereby changes may be made from time to time.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Will the minister tell me something of the terms of leases affecting lands under the control of the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I have
just mentioned that.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: I thought you were discussing the provincial rules.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: I was at the outset, but I pointed out that we reserved the right to change the regulations at any time as to Dominion lands.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The stumpage charged by
the Dominion may vary, I suppose from year to year? The right is reserved under the lease to charge whatever the current rate of stumpage may be?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Oh, yes.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Then in what way is the
holder of an old license placed at a disadvantage compared with the man who gets a license to-day? As I understand the system, it is simply that permission is given to cut on a certain area, payment to be made at the current rate of stumpage for whatever is taken off. I do not see where there is any greater burden one way or the other, whether the lease is old or new- I followed with particular attention the evidence taken before the commission on pulpwood in New Brunswick and partly in Nova Scotia. While the pulp-wood commission was supposed to have one chief object in view, they deal with many kindred matters and I think a perusal of the evidence would be well worth while so far as suggestions are concerned. I took the opportunity to prepare for the commission and hand to them an abstract of the laws
of New Brunswick particularly directed to fire prevention. We have there not only the general law, but in some localities there is power to make more stringent regulations. What the minister says is absolutely correct, that if you have an area with very stringent regulations they will not be enforced because otherwise the producer in that section is put at a very distinct disadvantage when he has to bear the cost of carrying on fire protection as against some other area where the regulations are not so strictly enforced or where they do not exist. The comparison may not only be between provinces, but between sections of the same province. In a few words what I should like to say to the minister is this:	That while I have every possible sympathy with him in his idea as to regulation, yet I rather fear that we are, perhaps, scarcely getting at it from the right angle. You can have plentiful regulation, and I feel that is the position we are in in the province of New Brunswick, where our regulations are stiffer than they have been probably for a century, and yet our forests have been more devastated of recent years than they have been for a very long time previously. The trouble is that our regulations remain on the paper where they are printed and it is difficult -and I know it is a tremendous subject-to get the regulations enforced. The minister is going to experience that difficulty and so is everybody else who is engaged in forest protection. The employment of aeroplanes is useful so far as the detection of fires is concerned but it is only a palliative. After the fire has started I grant the aeroplane can discover it, and I am going to discountenance in any way the use of the aeroplane, but the trouble is that that fire has started. In some cases it starts through natural agencies like a stroke of lightning, but ordinarily it starts through human influence. That means campers, or picnickers, or hunters, or careless people engaged in forest operations. Now it is very difficult to get at the campers, the picnickers and the hunters. We have regulations in New Brunswick whereby you can get at the hunter but you cannot possibly track him. You cannot control the operator without the necessity of imposing a tremendous burden on him in carrying out stringent regulations, a burden so heavy that he cannot compete with people who do not have to face those regulations. I have sympathy with the minister in trying to work up what I might call a Dominion standard and trying to get it accepted, but the Dominion standard alone without a punch behind it will not be of very much value. Our
Supply-Interior

people have to realize that laws must be enforced and that is one of the difficulties at the present time-that laws are considered to be something made to be placarded, to be read, everything except to be obeyed in the spirit as well as in the letter. That is the greatest trouble I believe with our forest protection. It is all very well to talk about reforestation. I agree with the minister we do not need it in most localities, the thing is to save the existing forests. And always bear in mind when we talk about reproduction of the forest that it is being reproduced in areas that are largely outside of the reach of the present generation, at great distances from water communication and from rail communication; the affected portion of the forest we are dealing with is in a comparatively limited area, and the timber is disappearing with tremendous rapidity. Now, the question arises, is the country prepared to save what it has? In order to do it there must be Dominion-wide effort and we must have absolute enforcement of the law. It will increase the price of raw material, but there is such a demand in the country to-day for our wood products that the purchasers can and must afford to pay the price that is necessary in order to preserve the heritage of the people of the Dominion. We are not losing wood alone. Everybody must notice from time to time the reports of devastation caused by wind, storm and rain, and all that kind of thing, which has a direct, immediate effect on forest waste that it will take more than one generation to restore.
Mr. RYCIvMAN:	Would the minister
kindly tell us what portion of last year's vote was expended for the province of Ontario?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: We do not spend any money in Ontario except $20,000 on research work. Each of the provinces assumes the responsibility of caring for its own resource. The main reason we discuss this in the provinces at all is for the purpose of propaganda, in the hope that we will- be able to encourage people to take a greater interest in this resource.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Is this money all spent in the three prairie provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: And British Columbia.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Have you any figures to
illustrate the extent of the devastation from fire that takes place in the three prairie pro-fMr. Baxter.]
vinces and British Columbia? I understood from an article to which the minister's name was signed that the annual loss was about $15,000,000.

Can the minister give

Mr. STEW'ART (Argenteuil):	The forest
reserves gave us a revenue last year of $143,000, but that does not take into account the receipts from the timber licenses because that is only from the lands set aside by the federal government as forest reserves. maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Has the hon. minister
the number of feet cut upon the forest reserves and the number of licenses?

are:

Mr. ARTHURS' Do the licensees pay 8ny sums towards fire protection?

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Timber dues for 1922-23 on license cuts amounted to S825 -COO.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Does that include the
stumpage?

Supply-Interior

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Total revenue.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That was
the total revenue.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
One piece of timber is
sold under auction, and tenders are received. Does that item include what is received under the method of sale of disposition of timber?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Yes, it is
included in the year in which the money is paid over. It is the bonus my hon. friend has reference to paid for the privilege of doing the work.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That is included in the
fees.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
In view of the statement
made by the hon. member for St. John and Albert (Mr. Baxter), in regard to the fires and their control, could the minister tell us whether there was any noticeable improvement in the prairie provinces and British Columbia where the lands are under federal legislation?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Yes, there
is a very marked improvement. We had little loss last year. As my hon. friend knows, conditions make some difference. If we have a year of heavy rainfall the hazard is not so great. That being the case, last year naturally it was reduced almost to a minimum, but the average goes to show that we are not allowing the fires to get away. They are small in character, and do not cause the damage they did formerly.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Can the minister allocate the appropriation to the different provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I do not
know that we can do that. That, of course, would apply in British Columbia for example, just to the railway belt.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I am satisfied with the
minister's words, is so far as they evidence an interest in the subject and a realization of its imminent importance, indeed a realization of the peril we are under at the present time. I cannot say that I am very much encouraged by the relation of practical achievements, much less by the disclosure of practical plans of improvement. He tells us that they purpose using the aeroplanes of the Defence forces. Well, I do not know that there is very much to be hoped for there. I do not know just the extent of the air service that is being maintained. If it is.gradually going 80
out of existence, as is the case with other services, it will not be of very much value lo the forests or anything else. I would like to have some idea of the plan by which we are going to effect a radical improvement in the survey and general supervision of our forests; that is to say, what further use is to be made of the aeroplanes, what further use is to be made of the telephone, or what steps are being taken to counteract the bud worm and other pests and diseases? I think the minister's figures as to the loss by fire are low indeed relatively to the loss by nature and while he hopes, without revealing to the House any comprehensive scheme or plan for taking the situation in hand, to reduce our fire loss by half in two years, he is actually confronted with the fact that the loss is increasing every year right under his eyes, and pretty much under the exact policy he is following now.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Not in the
area the federal government controls.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Was the loss last year
less than the year before?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: We had few fires there.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Perhaps not in that area, but in the whole of Canada it was greater. Our losses were colossal in eastern Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
It may be the minister
was fortunate last year, and it may be that the results were a testimony of the efficiency of the system we had. I fear myself it is more a testimony to good luck. What steps is the minister taking to prevent settlement in districts that should not be open to settlement?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That was
settled last year by the Forests Act.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
And settlers are not
going in?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Outside of those areas,
are steps being taken to discourage, or even to prohibit, settlement in districts where the harm the settler will do will be greater than the benefit to himself or the country? I think that settlement is one of the major causes of our forest devastation. Furthermore, as the minister said, in respect of one or two of the railway ventures we are entering into, the danger from fire by the penetration of those roads is greater than the possible hope of benefit. I have in mind the

Supply-Interior

Guysborough line for example. It runs through considerable timber, and I fancy from what I have heard it will likely burn down more timber than will be compensated for by all the good it will ever do. I hear someone laughing. I fancy he knows the circumstances. Information about that is coming to hand all the time, but I do not want to drift into a discussion on that subject. But in respect to prairie lines, in mapping out the direction, especially of the northern lines, has the subject been taken into account? We have lost by the penetration of railways, some of them unnecessary, to the extent of hundreds of millions. We have lost timber worth more than the railways of this country are worth	or ever will be worth.
The way timber has been destroyed by the penetration of more or less useful railways is simply a crime. In all these respects, not only a comprehensive, but a determined, persistent policy must be maintained. I do not think the reproduction is going to take care of our fire losses or our cut by any means unless a tremendous improvement is effected. I was criticised because in a speech this session 1 said that we were engaged to-day in the depletion of our irreplaceable losses, virtually selling our estate, that is in respect of our timber, and that when it was gone, it would take generations to replace it. An hon. member said that that was an exaggeration. An exaggeration! It is an understatement. I have talked with as good experts as we have in the countiy. I know that the time required for trees to grow varies, and the exact time for any class at any certain point is not even then very closely determined. The engineers of our larger companies differ in that regard; but I have never heard any of them put at under fifty years, the time for even the most rapidly growing trees to come to any sort of maturity. Some of them very much longer, double the time. Therefore, when one places at a generation the time required to replace the whole that we destroy, he is making a very modest statement of the truth, so that the attention we have given to the subject is altogether too little in proportion to its consequences.
I know the minister's difficulties; they are largely those difficulties that grow out of our federal constitution, and consequently to overcome them, not only co-operation by convention and by word of our provinces must be maintained, but actual results in the way of uniform regulations and uniform schemes of protection must be arrived at and pursued. It is the last few years that have brought this home to us as never hefore. We have developed all through the last decade or so

quite a considerable fire-fighting force in the federal service, but it is in the last three or four years that we have found ourselves face to face with a very critical position. I do not think those who take the gloomiest view of the near approach of our forest destitution are very far out. All the minister can do to bring the facts home to the people of Canada, he ought to do, and any moneys carefully spent to that end, or rather moneys wisely spent to that end, for wisdom is better than even care there, will be amply repaid to the people of the Dominion. We have to bring home not only the inportance of this matter to every person who cares for his country, but the wisdom to the individual of taking care of it to save himself. What I mean is this: I think we need a few very drastic punishments in this country for fire starting. I do not know of any better way to bring the necessity home to some people than that way, or, indeed,	any way except that	way.	Wehave not	had it.	We have	had	aleniency on the part of courts, and we have had	a general	laxity on	the	partof public opinion with the consequence that just what	an offence	in respect	of forest
destruction really means has never been brought home to the reckless and semicriminal. That is essential, and I think the minister can help in that regard. He ought sometimes to be represented at trials that we may have in our country to endeavour to impress our courts with what this thing really means and what the people and government of Canada consider to be a matter of importance.

As a matter of fact, in our forest reserves, it is almost necessary to send a fire ranger after any party that goes through for fear fires are neglected and incipient fires start as a result of carelessness on the part of campers. I think that is the experience at every one of the forest departments of provincial governments- Perhaps my right hon. friend is right in saying that the rainfall assisted us very materially last year, but I need only instance the year before last when we had such a tremendous loss in British Columbia. I am glad of this discussion and I believe it is well worth while, because I think with the minister that a developed public opinion is the most effective safeguard against fires, and I am speaking from some personal experience which I have had in a forest reserve in my own district, the Rocky Mountain House Reserve. I have noted there in the last few years a very marked change in public sentiment, so that to-day it is looked upon by the people of the district as rather a heinous crime to let fires go. With the growth of this sentiment I have observed a diminution in fires, and I think that the more the importance of the matter is emphasized the better.
Under this item I want to call the attention of the minister to the situation in that forest reserve. I intended bringing it up last year under the public works votes, but I was ruled out of order. There is, in that reserve about 20 miles within the boundary, a mining town known as Nordegg with a population of 1,500. It is related to the Brazeau collieries, one of the big steam coal collieries, and it lies about 180 miles west of Red Deer. From Red Deer to Hol-berg, 40 miles east of Nordegg, there is a provincial road, but from Holberg to Nordegg there is no road at all. In other words, there is a stretch of some 40 mlies which is provided with neither road nor telephone, and the only communication the people have with the outside world is by train three times a week. You can realize what an inconvenience this is to a town of 1,500, a great many of whom are married men. There is no possible communication by road unless one goes by pack horse, if one understands how to use it. The difficulty is that 20 miles of the 40 are under provincial jurisdiction, the other 20 being within the province of the Dominion. The province itself certainly would not undertake road construction through a federal reserve and these people have petitioned time and again to have a road built. They have generally petitioned the provincial government, under a misapprehension as to the peculiar situation that exists in connection with this divided jurisdiction. There is opportunity

Supply-Interior
for a great deal of business to be done; and apart from the inconvenience and the discomfort which necessarily attach to life under these conditions, these people have no means of leaving home except by train. There is a very good mixed farming country not very far east from Nordegg, and the people grow enough fresh vegetables and produce sufficient butter, milk and so forth to supply the needs of the town. They could be taken in and delivered very conveniently by car or truck. A road through there would help the people of Nordegg and the farmers in the surrounding country, and would build up business generally. While I realize that the engineering problem may be difficult and expensive as Nordegg lies in the foothills, at the same time I think it would be advisable for the minister to discuss the matter with his colleagues, because other departments may be involved in such road construction, and to confer with the provincial authorities with a view to arriving at some working arrangement under which this forty-mile stretch of road might be constructed. I believe it can be done; but if not, I would ask him to at least consider the granting of permission to the people there to build a telephone line and so enable them to have telephone connection with the outside world. As I understand the regulations, telephone lines are not allowed in the forest reserves except for the use of the forestry officials, and the railways will not permit telephone wires to be strung on their poles except for official use. The result is that the people of Nordegg. although only forty miles from telephone service, are as absolutely cut off from it as if they were in the South Sea islands. I would ask the minister to take these two matters under consideration to see if some relief cannot be afforded these people.

If the soil is sandy, of course nothing further will be done, but if it is of a character that will lend itself to agriculture, then the investigation is made and the cost ascertained. I have given my hon. friend what the low minimum value would be, namely, ten dollars an acre, but in all probability, when the land is thoroughly drained and dried, the surrounding land would be worth twenty or twenty-five dollars an acre.

speechtext: That remains to be seen. I do not think at the moment the land could be sold. When water has lain for generations on land it leaves the surface in an unsatisfactory state for agriculture, and it will take some years to dry it. I meant to see it last year but I have never been able to see it. My information is that when a few years have passed and the ditches have been kept open and the drainage properly attended to, it will be first-class agricultural land.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE

speechtext: There are two services joined together. There is the Water Power branch that was created some years ago. As a matter of fact, the Reclamation service, owing to the reason that [DOT] I gave to my hon. friend, is being amalgamated with the Water Power branch. The main work of this branch now is stream measurement and investigation for power purposes throughout the whole of Canada. That was carried on under Mr. Challies. The water-power investigation I deem to be of the greatest importance to the country, and I would commend any reasonable expenditure for carrying on that investigation. But the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. McQuarrie) has raised a point. We want to find out whether or not the expenditure being incurred is bringing returns and whether the country is warranted in continuing it. That seems to me the vital point as regards drainage work. If it is going to take years for these lands to dry out and to get rid of the sourness so as to become valuable, and if these drains have to be kept open in the meantime, I should be inclined to think that, in the end, they would cost more than they were worth, even though they sold at the same value as surrounding land that had been properly drained in the past.	.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I would
not like to venture my opinion, but I never was an enthusiast about drainage. When I was in the Alberta legislature, I set my face rigidly against it, except, perhaps, for the purpose of draining a road allowance. We have millions of acres of first class land there still unsettled, and until those lands are all absorbed, I think it is premature to do this work. I thought, however, that we were, in duty bound-I	am now speaking of the
period when we took office-to finish up the survey work in connection with irrigation. We are spending a little on that this year but the work is practically completed. It is not my intention to spend any money on reclamation projects at all, much less to think of attempting, under the control of the Dominion government, to drain the lands. I give my hon. friend every assurance on that ground, but this department will now develop mainly into a department for investigations into power, which, my hon. friend will agree with me, is most important in Ontario and Quebec, as well as in the other provinces of Canada. Reliable data on that score is most important, because no one can anticipate how rapid the development will be of our power resources. They have developed very rapidly in the past, and I hope that rapid development will continue in the future. We shall be able to furnish very reliable data to investors who propose to go in and develop the water-powers that are found throughout Canada. We are doing not only hydrometric work, but making power measurements as well.
