speechtext: We have been asked to investigate the possibilities of power development by the tide in the bay of Fundy.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: That would be at the reversible falls in St. Johnj but I am referring to inland waters two hundred miles from the mouth of the river at a place called Grand Falls. The province of New Brunswick proposes developing that power in the near future and I was wondering whether the department had been asked to inquire into the possibilities at that point and what the results were.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
We have
not made any investigation but we are making stream measurements on that river.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: What method does the department follow? Does it indiscriminately measure certain rivers, or does it do so upon the request of the province?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: We have an arrangement with the power commission of New Brunswick and whatever work is done in the way of measurements is carried on by virtue of that arrangement.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Is it done at their
request?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I should
think it would not be done unless they requested it.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: That is rather a difficult question to answer because this work is done co-operatively between the two staffs, and we have no definite allocation of work except in so far as there is an arrangement between the staffs working on these projects.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Judging from the work
done in those provinces that control their own natural resources, what value has been

Supply-Interior
placed upon that work by the Dominion from the standpoint of its reliability? Further' has any development taken place- or have any surveys been made independently of those carried on by the provinces themselves?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I do not
see how any development could take place in connection with stream measurement, because, as I have pointed out half a dozen times, it is a matter of considerable years of careful measurements before definite data can be obtained. The following is a letter from Mr. P. J. Veniot, the Premier of New Brunswick, with respect to this matter:
The question of providing funds for carrying on the co-operative stream measurement and water power investigations of the Maritime provinces under the direction of the Water Power branch of your department, is no doubt now under consideration. I am aware that particular attention is being given to the necessity for rigid economy in federal matters this year, but in so far as this province is concerned.
I desire to impress upon you the desirability to have this work continued along the same lines and to the same extent as it is at present being carried on. Unless this work is carried on as heretofore, some other arrangement must be made, as it is essential to the hydro electric development, which we are now carrying on in this province and I feel convinced that it will be admitted without question, that in the interests of real economy for the country as a whole, the development of hydro electric energy is a necessity which it i* found to be economically possible. It is obvious that stream measurement work and water power investigations can be carried on more economically under the present co-operative arrangement than if our province attempted to set up a separate organization of its own. There is also the advantage that records of information of this nature obtained by your department are co-ordinted as to the accuracy and form with similar ncords throughout other parts of Canada. Engineers and official people interested in the hydro development are familiar with the methods of your department and they accept your records more readily and quickly than if they were obtained by organizations not so well known to them. This province highly appreciates the efforts made by your department in the past. You are no doubt aware that during the past few years this province has carried on hydro electric development up to the present time to a total investment of $3,500,000. We are now embarking upon the development of what is known as the Grand Falls proposition, which will ensure for this province cheap power and light and cost in the vicinity of $7,000,000. The data connected with the power already developed, as well as with the power now contemplated, would not have been possible without the assistance made available by the co-operative arrangements under discussion. I am sure that, informed as you are, in relation to this whole matter, you will be satisfied that a continuance of the present small expenditure in this province by your department is justified and that you will have no difficulty in persuading your colleagues to the same opinion.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Has the department
made any surveys on the Musquash development in New Brunswick which is being undertaken by the provincial government?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Yes, there
was co-operation as to data.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Does the survey include the amount of horse-power that might be developed at any given point on the river, or is it more in the nature of ascertaining the volume of continuous flow?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
It is more
to establish the dependable volume of flow. Then estimates can be made of the probable horse-power to be developed.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
What was the report
on the streams that form the Musquash development? It was questioned whether the volume of water would justify such development.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I think it
would be better if the engineer in charge sent the hon. member a full report of our investigation.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: It would save time.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: What investigation of hydropower development is going on in Ontario? There is evidence of possible shortage of power there, and therefore it is very important, that the provincial authorities should know what developments may be available.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Measurements are being taken on all the rivers in Ontario which may be capable of developing power.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The minister says that
measurements are being taken on "all the rivers.'' I presume investigations have been completed on many. But I was wondering what new ventures are in sight. For instance, I presume we have full knowledge now as to the total possible development on the Niagara, and in my own locality on the Severn river. But what other work is being carried on in this connection at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Measurements have been going on for only five years. As I have said repeatedly, that is not a sufficient time within which to provide definite data on which to base dependable flow, as the records vary very considerably. In ten or twelve years the dependable flow can be pietty well established, and this, after all, is the information which engineers seek in connection with development work.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Apart from storage, I suppose
the flow at low water is what is important. But I have not the slightest desire to get into a discussion upon the scientific features. I was merely wondering in what parts of Ontario this work was being carried on at the present time. Are these hydrometric tests being made now in Ontario?
Supply-Interior

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
On every
river in Ontario where there is a possibility of power development, but the tests have been carried on for a period of only five years. Ontario and Quebec are developing most rapidly in this connection. We have been working in conjunction with the Ontario government for the past five years. Of course at Niagara, for example, records have been kept for many years; in the northern portion of the province this is not so.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Take the minister's own county -which is also mine-there is only one development, that on the Severn river. I take it for granted that the possible power development there is well known now, and that consequently investigations are at an end. Are the present investigations all being conducted in northern Ontario?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I will hand
my hon. friend the list.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Is it so extensive?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Yes, it
covers about twenty. I will pass it over to my hon. friend.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: A few years ago the International Waterways Commission was formed and one of its members was appointed from New Brunswick. That commission made a report, one copy of which was sent to the authorities in the state of Maine and the other to the Department of the Interior here. I have on several occasions tried to get this report, but so far I have not succeeded. The Grand Falls waterpower is one of the largest in the Maritime provinces, and I am happy to say that it is about to be developed. In order to obtain authority for this purpose the provincial government must get permission from the Minister of the Interior, and also from the state of Maine.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Is it an international river?

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Yes. The falls are about two miles below the state of Maine, but as it is an international river naturally the waters are protected by both countries. I should like to get a copy of the report I have referred to. I may add that encouragement by the Dominion government in the development of this power would be welcomed by the people of New Brunswick.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
In this connection, do the surveys of the department include the possibility of maintaining the flow of the river by adequate storage dams at the point

of development? With respect to the question put by the hon. member for Restigouche and Madawaska (Mr. Michaud), I understand it is necessary to get authority from the state of Maine or from the American government to build storage dams on the St. John river north of Grand Falls in the United States. Will it be the duty of the Dominion government or of the provincial government to secure such authority? In other words, has the provincial government power to negotiate with a neighbouring country for storage rights? We must ajso secure similar rights from the province of Quebec. The St. John river is the international boundary from a point about two miles north of Grand Falls almost to its source; but where the actual development will take place is entirely within the Dominion.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: If it is international water, an agreement of course, would have to be executed between the two federal governments. So far as provincial storage is concerned there is no reason why the two provinces could not work that out by agreement.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: I presume, then, that any storage needed in the state of Maine would have to be the subject of negotiation through the federal governments?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
In that case I would like to urge on the minister the necessity of cooperation. Our provincial government propose, I believe, to go ahead and develop this power. It is one of the hopes of the future of New Brunswick that we should have cheap power to manufacture our pulpwood and our hardwood timber, which cannot be floated down the rivers and which is too heavy to ship by rail in the raw state; indeed, it should not be shipped out of the country in the raw state anyway. We have immense resources of hardwood timber that can and will be manufactured if we can get cheap power. That particular power site is the best in New Brunswick, possibly the second best in Canada, next only to Niagara. But it is an international waterway, and we must get storage rights in Maine as well as in Quebec in order to maintain a flow in the river, because at low water there is not a sufficient flow to permit the continuous production of power. It is a mighty river in freshet time, and there are great lakes available that can be dammed so as to hold immense quantities of water which can be used to feed the river in times of drought. I would urge upon the minister the necessity of co-operating with our government in the matter.

Supply-Interior

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: The present purpose of the provincial government is to develop a certain amount of power at Grand Falls, and that can be done without any international negotiation at all.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: That is, in the initial stages.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Yes. Speaking from memory,
I believe about 40,000 horse power can be developed without any interference with either the state of Maine or the province of Quebec. If it is found desirable to go further by the building of higher dams or the storing of more water for flowage purposes, it will then be necessary to make arrangements with the state of Maine and the province of Quebec. The matter is being investigated by the provincial authorities through the Hydro-
11 p.m. Electric Commission there, and it has been taken up, I understand, with the Minister of the Interior as . regards measurements, requirements, and so on. But I feel that no difficulty of the kind suggested can possibly arise in connection with the present development at Grand Falls.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: I thoroughly agree with my hon. friend, but I feel that it would not be advisable for the provincial government to proceed even in the initial stages of the development without the assurance that they can get these storage nights, because the ultimate aim is to develop much more power than can be developed from the natural run of water and from the storage facilities available in New Brunswick alone. If the initial development takes place without the understanding that we can .get this water storage if we need it, there might come a time when, in order to further our project or to prevent its development from being heldup, we would have to make concessions that we would not wish to make. I am sure however that the federal department will cooperate with the province of New Brunswick in any effort along this line.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Would the minister be good enough to tell the committee briefly the exact position of the application with respect to power development from the Spray lakes in Banff National Park and whether or not he is considering its rejection in the interests of the preservation of the national parks-that is, free from industrial interference, and so on? That I think is the policy in the great national parks of the United States, and I know is the policy approved by a great many people who have given close study to the matter of the preservation of our national parks in their natural state. It is a very important question
and one that really should be discussed at length. I merely hint at these things; the minister will recognize at once what I refer to. Without delaying the committee with tiresome details, I would just like to put my question in that way.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The situation at the moment is that there is before the department an application on behalf of the Calgary Power Company, who get their power from the Kananaskis falls on the Bow river. We have been carrying on hydrometric measurements on the Bow river, though we have somewhat delayed the work; however, that is somewhat apart from my hon. friend's question. There is no doubt that the Calgary Power Company will require additional power; indeed, their supply will have to be more than doubled if they are to meet the demands made upon them by the municipality of Calgary. They have made application for the Spray lakes basin as a storage reservoir. The park superintendent and park authorities are very much opposed to the development of this power within the park.
I have a perfectly open mind upon it. I went to the park to see the place for myself and to get first-hand information with regard to the situation. As my hon. friend knows, we have a very large area appropriated for park purposes at Banff. There are several hundred miles of roadway through that area, and all kinds of scenery. The road leading up to Mount Assiniboia, which would pass this development, is not one of the most scenic roads one couldi find though the valley in the vicinity of Mount Assiniboia is undoubtedly one of the sights of Banff park. I am not prepared to say that this development would mar the appearance of the park to any considerable degree, but I have a great deal of sympathy with the idea that these areas should be preserved as playgrounds for the people, and anything that would impair their beauty or their interest I would feel like opposing. As I say, I do not think the development would interfere very materially with the park as such, in view of the fact that it comprises so many hundreds of thousands of acres and is characterized by such varied scenery. Since the application of the Calgary Power Company was received the province of Alberta has become interested in power development and they also have made a formal application for this storage basin. We have given them the same answer that we gave the power company; that we do not want to enter hastily into an agreement. The effect of the development on the
Supply-Interior

park, on its scenic beauty, and its effect also in the way of precedent for the future, are things which w'ould have to be given very careful consideration. The Alberta government wish to verify the statement of our engineers and of the engineers of the power company as to the volume to be stored and the value of the storage basin for power purposes, and they intend to make an independent investigation on their own behalf. Of course, if the province wishes to enter into a hydro project, and if it is believed desirable to grant the request of anyone in this regard, the province would be given the preference. But though I cannot say that I think the scenery would be very much disturbed, the question of establishing a precedent is one which requires very careful consideration before a privilege of this kind is granted to anyone.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: I would like to make a request of the minister. I have no particular right to do so, except that I am intensely interested in the general question of the preservation of the national parks. I would ask that nothing be done in this matter within the coming year so that ample opportunity may be given for pondering the question, for its consideration not only by the minister's department but by the public, who, after all, are really more affected than even the government itself. I gather from the minister's remarks that the power company still have some units that they can develop on the Bow river site, so that there is no need for great haste at this time.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
And plenty
of coal.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Exactly. Having these things in mind I think it would be a very fine thing if the government would declare that for a period of a year nothing will be done, and then in the interim let public opinion adjust itself and familiarize itself with all the circumstances. I think we would all be in a better position to judge of the merits of the case at the end of another year. On the other hand, I may say this, that even if there is a desire on the part of the government to come to an ultimate decision on it in the near future, personally I would hesitate before agreeing to this item without the privilege of discussing it at great length and threshing the whole matter out. That I do not wish to do at the moment, and I think if the minister could give the assurance asked it would be the happiest way out of the difficulty at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I think I
can give my hon. friend at once that assurance. I am not in any hurry to deal with this particular question because I think it is of such importance.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: I should like to support the request of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens). It is a matter in which I feel intensely interested. It is important that these national parks should be preserved for the public. Shortly before coming to Ottawa I was waited upon by some of my constituents who felt very strongly upon this subject. I think a policy should be pursued as would preserve these places of natural beauty as much as possible for the use of the people unimpaired, and I am quite satisfied that the public generally would very strongly resent the idea that these parks should be alienated from public use to serve the purposes of a commercial company.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: I should like to inform the minister that the whole Alpine Club of Canada is watching this application with jealous eyes. They believe there should be no interference with the Spray river park such as would detract in any way from the attractive and pleasureable features which make these national parks so desirable as playgrounds for the people. I think the government should formulate a policy respecting the national parks so that no unfortunate precedent would be created for the future.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The granting of water
power privileges on Spray lakes is, of course, a very important matter. The minister says that he does not want to establish a precedent. As a matter of fact a precedent has already been established because the Calgary Power Company	hold water power
privileges within the park area right at this moment. However, I do think this parliament should take definite steps to formulate a policy so far as the parks are concerned and determine finally whether it is the intention to allow industrial development within the park area. I think the matter should be carefully considered and then, in the light of the action that parliament takes, it will be time enough to determine what industrial development should be allowed. There is a further thing in connection with this particular matter. I do not believe that any private company should be given power privileges within the park. I think that whatever rights are going to be granted for industrial purposes should be granted to the provincial government or should be conducted under some system of government

Supply-Interior
ownership or government control. For after all while it is quite true as the minister has said, that the particular area around the Spray lakes is not now of much scenic value -except perhaps in the case of the lakes themselves and the Spray river falls-still if they were allowed to come under private control there can be no doubt that those interests would be primarily concerned in getting their money out of the project and getting it as rapidly as possible; whereas if the development were under government control the government would also be interested in maintaining the park value of the area involved in which the power privileges exist. I trust that the minister will not be hasty in granting the request of the Calgary Power Company. Under any circumstances I do not think it should be granted, but if the province feels that this is an enterprise which might profitably be undertaken without in any way imperilling that area as a park asset, then on that matter I will have an open mind; but certainly I would not support the application of the Calgary Power Company under any circumstances.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
There is
one other matter I should like to call to the attention of the minister before we pass this item. He has made a statement this evening in regard to his general attitude or policy on reclamation projects, to the effect that he does not believe it is a good policy at this time to reclaim lands for their intrinsic value for agricultural purposes. In so far as that statement goes I am wholly in accord with the minister, but I want to point out the fact to the minister that there are large districts in western Canada where drainage projects have to be instituted if the land is to be properly settled. In these areas drainage projects have to be instituted and carried out before school districts can be established and roads built. Very often these projects are beyond the scope of the new municipalities within which they must be undertaken. In the province of Saskatchewan I am aware that the provincial government has made arrangements to take over enterprises of this kind, place them on a sound financial basis, and carry them to completion, making the land pay for the work put upon it when it has been reclaimed. However, it is a fact, and it can well be understood why this is the case, that these lands that have to be reclaimed are very largely lands that are still vested in the Crown, or that being in need of drainage have not been taken up by the settlers entering the country. Now, rightly or wrongly the opinion prevails in 81
many of the districts where this drainage has to be carried out that the regulations of the Department of the Interior constitute a hindrance and make it very difficult for these schemes to be carried out by the provincial department of highways which has charge of them. The statement of the minister as to his being wholly against reclamation projects would perhaps lend additional colour to the complaints that are made. Therefore I think it would be only fair for him to state the policy of his department in that regard, and make it plain as to whether his department is endeavouring to do what it can to render easier the carrying out of these projects where they are absolutely necessary, or whether the departmental officials are placing all the hindrances they can in the way of permitting Crown lands to be included in reolamatictn projects.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
No, the
situation is quite the reverse. All these Crown lands that are found within a drainage area in which a province or municipality is desirous of establishing a reclamation scheme are sold at a dollar an acre-preferably to the province, I think altogether to the province because they take them in charge and they are to be sold under the same regulations as the school lands. However, every acre of Crown land that is found within one of these drainage areas can be had for the benefit of the area at a dollar an acre. Then, of course, provincial drainage laws affect the scheme. There can be no opposition on the part of the federal government. What I want to make clear is, that so far as the federal government is concerned I would not venture into the Water-hen project or anything of that character. That is what I want to make clear.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
May I ask the
minister, in regard to these measurements, if the results of the investigations are printed.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: I can furnish my hon. friend with the flowage on each river.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The Madawaska
and the Sydenham are the only two rivers I am interested in.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
In connection with the matter of reducing the staff, so far as dismissals have been necessary, is any priority given to returned soldiers? I understand that sometime ago the hon. Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) indicated that it would be the attitude of the government, so far as possible,

Supply-Interior

to see that returned soldiers were retained in employment if dismissals became necessary owing to reduction of staff. Does that same practice apply to the Water Power branch?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: In the staff reduction which is going on, the practice my hon. friend refers to applies to a returned soldier, if he has the minimum qualifications. The returned soldier is given the preference, unless there is some very grave reason why it cannot be done.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Would the minister inform the House as to what the government's *programme in British Columbia is for the coming year under this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I will be
glad to give my hon. friend this same information in regard to the rivers in British Columbia.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Under this vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: You are going to measure the rivers set out in this list?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Is there anything else on your programme?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: No. These rivers are provincial.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: I am asking what the programme is, and the minister hands me a list with the names of a lot of rivers, and that is the programme. Now that is not the programme, because other expenditures are to be made in British Columbia. I would like to ask the minister what that programme is.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I am glad to see the reduction of $104,000 in this vote. I brought the matter' as forcibly as I could to the attention of the House last year, and I stated that it was beyond the understanding of a great many people in the eastern provinces that those large amounts should be spent on irrigation, measurement of streams, geodetic surveys, boundary line surveys and so on. That expenditure is increasing every year. Now some of them, my hon. friend says, are good things. Well, some of them are. I understand from my hon. friends on the other side of the House that irrigation has been very beneficial. What we in the eastern provinces sometimes complain of is the development of water powers by this government or by any federal government. I think it is the province of any company that wishes to take up the matter to develop these 
water powers. Any company that would go into an enterprise of that kind should make their, own surveys, I think. I am glad that we have a reduction of this item, and I am pleased to hear from the minister that in the course of a few years it will be wiped out.
Som hon. MEMBERS: Carried.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: I understand the minister is getting information.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I cannot
give my hon. friend any more information than I gave to my hon. friend from Simcoe (Mr. Boys). This work involves the measurement of the rivers to ascertain flowage, in some cases for irrigation purposes, as the hon. member well knows, because the investigation is a varied one. In some cases it may be for drainage, but in most cases for the development of power, to establish definitely what power we can develop on these rivers, and in order that, if development is necessary-and in most cases it is at least projected-you may have definite data. This work is not so many dollars spent on a certain river. I cannot give that detail. But there are $47,000 all told in this vote to be spent, I think, in British Columbia for the purpose of getting data for the power people in your provincial government, the same as in any other province.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That is absolutely
not an answer to the question, and this document which the minister sent over does not answer the question; on the contrary it is something altogether different, and it so states. The heading is:
Rivers covering which studies have been made of power possibilities.
That does not answer my question at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
May I tell
the hon- gentleman again-and I hope this time he will remember-that it does not involve measurements for one year, or two-years, or three years, or four years, or five years, or six years, or seven years, or eight years, or nine years, or ten years, or eleven years, or twelve years; but it is a continued study that must be earned on, if you are to have reliable data for the purposes for which the measurement is being made. Have I made it clear to my hon. friend?

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I should say not. 1
am sorry the minister finds it necessary to lose his temper.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The minister has not lost his temper.

Supply-Interior

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Well he gives a very
good imitation of a man who has lost his temper. I do not think that I, or any hon. member in this group, have asked one question that was not a reasonable question, and one to which we were not entitled to an answer. I for one do not propose to allow these estimates to be railroaded through this House.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: I did not suggest they had been railroaded through. I think my question is a fair one and I am not endeavouring to obstruct. There is no reason why I should obstruct, but I asked what the government programme was in British Columbia for the coming year under this item, and what do I get? I receive a list of names of rivers on which studies have been made. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that is not an answer to the question at all.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: The hon. minister declares he has given certain information, and he is not required to repeat that information.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I do not suggest that
the hon. minister is required to repeat the information. I do not want him to repeat it, because he has not answered the question. I am now asking for an answer to the question, and if the minister feels tired and cannot understand a question when it is asked, we can allow this item to stand over till another time.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Would the
statement, that the definition at the top is misleading answer my hon. friend; that it is not merely for past measurements that he has the group of rivers, but for past, present and future measurements, the future covering, at the moment, only this year.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I will try again in
another way. How much of this item of $547,000 is to be spent in British Columbia?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
How is that $47,000
going to be spent, with the details?

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
By handing the money
to those who are entitled to it.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: Carried.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I do not think the minister has treated the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. McQuarrie) quite right. There is a fairness in the request, whatever may be said of any other question asked to-night. The request is for some details, which are usually given immediately, as to what is the intention in the disbursement of 81i
this $47,000. "Let me point this out to the minister. I had no intention of bringing it to his notice, but I do not think it is fair for hon. members to call "carried" when an hon. member is asking questions, and it is not a way to facilitate the passage of items.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
It has been done in the
past.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
A statute was passed in
1913, I think, whereby the water-powers in British Columbia or in the railway belt were turned over to the British Columbia government for administration. That creates a situation in British Columbia unique and entirely different from that obtaining in every other province. While the federal government owns or controls the water-powers in the railway belt, it parted with that control under the statute to the province of British Columbia. If I re 3all correctly, British Columbia maintains a water-power department, or it did a few years ago, doing very much the same work as this department is doing. It is interesting to us to know just what this $47,000 of federal money is to be applied to. Is it duplicating expenditures by the province? Is it a necessary expenditure? Is it possible to dispense with this expenditure by the federal government, and under the statute to allow the provincial government to do this class of work? As a matter of fact, $47,000 may not be very much to some hon. gentlemen who are calling "carried" and such like, but it is a sum worthy of consideration. This is a good time to pause and examine. The request of my hon. friend is for some information how the money is to be expended.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: In the first place, in order to answer my hon. friend as to co-operation, what he has said is perfectly correct. British Columbia, like the other provinces in Canada with which we are working in co-operation, is in control of its water-powers, and as to how far it is developing them, I have not the information.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: That is not what I refer to. I mean the relinquishment of Dominion control of water-porvers in the railway belt to the provincial government^ That was by a special act.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I quite
understand that; but this work, as my hon. friend well knows, is not confined to the railway belt; it covers the whole of the province. As in the case of the other province, I read a letter from Premier Veniot, perhaps a letter from Hon. T. D. Patullo,
Supply-Interior

Minister of Lands in British Columbia, would be of interest in order to give further information to my hon. friend. This letter reads:
The subject of stream measurements is of such far reaching importance in the provinces where hydro -power is capable of being developed or irrigation practised, as both are in this province, that I am constrained to venture some remarks on the national aspects of the question.
No resource of the country-not even agricultural or mineral lands-demands more careful investigation than the streams from which the water is derived for the development of power, for irrigation and for city water supply. While the physical aspects of agricultural and mining lands may be regarded as supremely stable the great water resources show daily, monthly and annual variations that require careful records extending over many years to demonstrate the quantities that may be depended on from any single source.
To secure uniformity of measurement, computation and tabulation and to provide reliability in comparison of streams throughout the Dominion it is equally necessary that the data be collected and published by the central authority.
If it is a matter of national importance-and it cannot be questioned-that agricultural experimental stations be established and other agricultural data be gathered and that geological surveys and investigations be made by the federal government, it is surely of equal national importance that a resource from which three and a quarter million horse-power are already developed and from which hundreds of thousands of acres of land are irrigated receive generous national support.
So far as this province is concerned it may be pointed out that its industrial life depends to a very large extent upon water power, and the agricultural resources of the whole interior of the province are dependent upon irrigation from its streams.
Handicapped to some extent by the lack of hydrometric data, the province, realizing the vital importance of stream measurement and gauge readings, was obliged to initiate the work some years ago. Apart altogether from any consideration of the national aspect of the question already referred to, the fact that many of its great streams and lakes were wholly or partly within the railway belt laid upon the Dominion the specific duty of investigating them. Accordingly it was arranged that the portion of the work which the province of necessity began was handed over to the federal organisation, the province making an annual money contribution for the service in lieu of direct expenditure.
In the efforts now being made for the reduction of national expenditures I trust that you will not permit of any change that will allow so necessary a service to be curtailed.
That is the view that the minister who is in charge of this work has of the question.
I think in fairness to British Columbia, it has a right to receive the same treatment as the other provinces of Canada are receiving in this respect, and I wish to assure my hon. friend that none of this work is undertaken unless there is a direct arrangement with the provincial authorities so that no overlapping in expenditure is going on.
I cannot give more definite data as to where work is being carried on than on the list which I passed over to my hon. friend, that is that we are making measurements on these 
streams for the very purpose mentioned by the minister, in order that reliable data may be had for development purposes.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: According to the list, that work is done.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Yes, I do
not know how many years we have been doing that, but most of this work has been under way for only five years. I do not know exactly how long because the minister intimates that the British Columbia government have been carrying on this work. Perhaps there. are some streams on which the data is complete, that is, on which accurate, reliable measurements have been kept for a period of twelve years. In that case there would be little or no need of continuing; but my hon. friend will agree that there is a great deal of work in British Columbia upon which the measurements have not been carried on for that period and upon which we are still continuing that work.
Further, my hon. friend knows that a good deal of controversy has been going on between the federal government, the provincial government and the Indians with respect to allocation of reserves, and measurement work has to be done there, in order that data may be available because, while it is not part of the settlement, because the settlement is largely that of land, work is being carried on there as well, that would be embodied rather fully in the report which I handed to my hon. friend, giving the rivers on which the work is being carried on, because the work is confined to those.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: To make my position perfectly clear, I want to assure the minister that I am not objecting to the expenditures in British Columbia or in any other province. I am simply endeavouring to do my duty in trying to get information as to how the money is to be spent. I am accepting the minister's statement to the effect that the work is going to be continued this coming year under an arrangement which has been or will be made with the province.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
This is a continuous arrangement with the province and does not end in any particular year. There is a standing agreement between the province and the federal .government for cooperation in this work, but my hon. friend should understand that reliable data of this character cannot be obtained under ten or twelve years. Perhaps there are some streams in regard to which the work is complete, but the great majority of them are probably

Capital Punishment
only half finished and measurements will have to go on for another period of years before reliable data will be completely secured.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: How many years has this work been going on?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: The agreement was executed on August 19, 1913.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: That is to say, eleven years. How many years longer has it to run?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext: As long as both parties are agreeable to its continuance.

maintopic: SECOND READINGS AND REFERENCE TO RAILWAY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
So that there is an arrangement under which the work is to be continued, and it is proposed to continue it this year. An arrangement, in other words, has been made or will be made as to all the work and that work will be confined to the rivers which were set out in the statement that the minister sent over to me. I think it is a commendable thing that the Dominion and the provinces should co-operate in such an important matter and I am not objecting to the arrangement. I hope the minister will not think that I am trying to harass him tonight or to obstruct his estimates.
Progress reported.
On motion of Mr. Mackenzie King the House adjourned at 11.40 p.m.
Friday, April 11, 1924
